text:
Fact Check: “Democrat insiders promised David Crowley $250,000 and a job for his wife in a Sara Rodriguez administration to get him out of the governor's race. He took the deal, exited the race, and endorsed Rodriguez the next [day].”

Bottom line: Unproven allegation.

Here's what can be verified:
✅ David Crowley did withdraw from the Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary in July 2026 and endorsed Sara Rodriguez the following day. Multiple news outlets reported both the withdrawal and immediate endorsement. [https://t.co/DxKSTdDs7j], [https://t.co/SmM75VTXoN], [wisconsine...aminer.com]
✅ A report by the Daily Wire alleged that a Democratic insider claimed Crowley agreed to leave the race in exchange for a promised $250,000 and a job for his wife in a future Rodriguez administration. The report says it relied on an unnamed party operative and "corroborating materials." [https://t.co/TEHYKa1pxz]
✅ Subsequent reports stated that an anonymous Democratic adviser allegedly signed an affidavit making similar claims. Those reports said the affidavit's authenticity was verified, meaning the affidavit exists and was signed. However, they did not establish that the alleged deal actually occurred. [https://t.co/KwbqJbJf0f], [https://t.co/rVYhIqjroq]
✅ Reports also note that the Crowley campaign denied the allegations. [https://t.co/KwbqJbJf0f], [wisconsinr...ghtnow.com], [https://t.co/rVYhIqjroq]

❌ There is currently no publicly available evidence showing that:

$250,000 was actually transferred,
a job was actually promised or offered,
Crowley accepted such a deal,
Rodriguez approved or participated in such an arrangement.
The sources reporting the allegation rely primarily on anonymous or unnamed insiders and have not published conclusive documentary proof establishing that the alleged agreement occurred. [https://t.co/TEHYKa1pxz], [https://t.co/KwbqJbJf0f], [https://t.co/rVYhIqjroq]

Verdict
Partly True / Unproven

True: Crowley exited the race and endorsed Rodriguez shortly afterward. [https://t.co/DxKSTdDs7j], [https://t.co/SmM75VTXoN], [wisconsine...aminer.com]

Unproven: The claim that he did so because Democratic insiders promised him $250,000 and a job for his wife remains an allegation, not an established fact. The existence of allegations and even a sworn affidavit does not by itself prove the underlying claim. [https://t.co/KwbqJbJf0f], [https://t.co/rVYhIqjroq]

A careful, evidence-based version would be:
"A Democratic insider alleged that David Crowley was offered $250,000 and a job for his wife in exchange for dropping out and endorsing Sara Rodriguez. Crowley and Rodriguez's camp deny the allegation, and no public evidence has independently verified that the alleged deal occurred." [https://t.co/TEHYKa1pxz], [https://t.co/KwbqJbJf0f], [https://t.co/rVYhIqjroq]

The Tribe - Part 5

Alliance

Rowena, the famously beautiful daughter of Hengist, sailed with the relief fleet. She was young, cunning, and absolutely committed to her father.  Soon after her arrival, Hengist arranged a great feast, and invited Vortigern and his leading nobles.  Rowena would spend the evening charming their guests and serving them copious amounts of wine and ale.  She paid considerable attention to Vortigern himself, and the king became enamored with her.  So much so in fact, that he asked for Rowena’s hand in marriage, and promised Hengist whatever he wished in return.

Following the feast, Hengist consulted with the Elders amongst the Saxons of Thanet.  The island was indeed getting crowded, yet few wished to leave as this new land promised much in the way of wealth and opportunity.  If anything the “Saxons” desired to expand.  Hengist sent word to Vortigern, and offered Rowena’s hand in marriage in exchange for Kent.  Vortigern agreed and Rowena became Vortigern’s second wife who he loved fiercely by all accounts.

Following the wedding, Saxons began settling in Kent, while Hengist and Horsa consolidated their hold on the new land.  For the Britons that wanted the Saxons to leave Thanet, they now saw instead even more of their lands given away to an increasing number of the foreigners.  Vortigern, their own Christian King even went so far as to forsake his wife and marry one of these pagan Saxons.  One can only imagine how Vortigern’s children felt about it.  The situation was at a boiling point.  Hengist took full advantage.  He entered directly into Vortigern’s household guard as chief advisor, and promised to protect his son and law the King, boasting that his people were “Stong, fierce, and born for war”.

But open conflict between the Saxons and the Britons who they relied on materially was not wise.  Hengist shrewdly offered Voritgern a solution that would re-direct all the simmering unease and potential violence outside of the realm, while at the same time providing for the Angles and Saxons whose upkeep the Britons now found too expensive.  

Hengist and his warriors would sail north of the Roman wall, into the land of the Picts and Scots.  He would be joined by an invasion fleet from the mainland led by his son Oisc.  Together they would invade the highlands, and avenge the suffering the Britons had endured for decades.  Vortigern agreed, and when Oisc arrived Hengist set sail with a combined fleet of 40 ships…

text:
Scientists put a dead chicken in a forest. Vultures gathered, then a carnivore lunged out of the trees | Discover Wildlife https://t.co/RUABpQCaFR
Writing in the Journal of Raptor Research, the scientists interpret the carnivore’s direct lunging posture as evidence of an opportunistic predation attempt. If that interpretation is correct, the encounter would be the first documented case of a greater grison trying to prey on a turkey vulture.

Most documented cases of vulture predation occur at nests, affecting eggs and nestlings; records involving adults are much rarer. “Few records involve adult vultures, likely because of their strong flight abilities and use of communal roosts,” say the authors in the study. That said, adult turkey vultures are not invulnerable, with a number of documented predation events in the Americas involving large raptors such as bald eagles and golden eagles, mammals such as raccoons and jaguars, and reptiles such as boa constrictors. 

The latest case was observed during a study on scavengers in Jama-Coaque Reserve, a private reserve in Ecuador’s Tumbes–Chocó–Magdalena biodiversity hotspot. As part of the study, the researchers placed a chicken carcass on the ground next to a tree and set up a camera trap in front of it.

The camera-trap images show three adult turkey vultures perched on the roots of the tree before a grison emerges from the undergrowth and lunges at them. The turkey vultures immediately take flight, along with a nearby black vulture. The grison then remains on the roots for around one minute, sniffing around the vultures’ perch, before disappearing out of shot.

The team believe this is the first known case of a direct attack attempt by a greater grison on a vulture. So, why did it do it?

“We ruled out the possibility of kleptoparasitism [where one animal steals food or prey from another] because the experimental carcass had been completely consumed before the recording began,” say the researchers. “Additionally, the grison showed no interest in the remains (bones and feathers) present at the site.”

Could the attack have been territorial? Greater grisons have previously been documented acting aggressively towards raptors during food consumption. Other mustelids (a family of carnivorous mammals to which the greater grison belongs) in Africa, such as the African striped weasel and the honey badger, are also known to confront larger species while displaying strong territoriality. However, in this instance, the researchers could neither prove nor disprove whether the attack was territorial because they were unable to gather additional photographic records of the grison in the area.

The researchers suggest that living in groups helped the vultures detect the threat and escape together, likely preventing the grison from pinning down a target. “Although group formation in vultures may increase competition for food, it also provides antipredator benefits by enhancing collective vigilance and reducing attack success… In our recorded case, group size likely improved vigilance and triggered the simultaneous flight of all individuals, making this strategy effective against potential predators.”

This rare encounter offers a glimpse of vulture foraging and vigilance strategies, as well as the behaviour of carnivores such as the greater grison. It also highlights how camera traps can reveal interactions that might otherwise go unseen – observations that contribute to understanding how food webs work in highly threatened ecosystems.

In the final chapter of this week's Torah portion, "Vayera," is Gen. 22, the Akeida, which means the binding of Isaac. Sometimes people wonder, how could God give His only Son to suffer a gruesome death. He did it for us, because of His great love, and Yeshua as the Son was willing to do it for the same reason. 

The akeida is an event that points to the suffering Messiah. God brought forth a miracle child, Isaac, born of a barren 90 yr old woman; and then commanded that very same miracle child to be sacrificed upon an altar. This is a prophetic teaching that points to Yeshua an even greater miracle child, born of a virgin, who is Savior of Mankind through His own shed blood.  In the Akeida we see the Father’s plan to give His own son as the sacrifice for the sins of the world.
· Gen. 22:2 - "Take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love." Like Isaac with Abraham, Yeshua is God's only begotten Son whom He loves. Abraham as the father is called to sacrifice his only son, whom he loves.  Isaac is called to give his life, which he was willing to do. God called it off, but left us with this prophetic picture of what He as the Father was going to do with His own Son for the salvation of Mankind.
· Mount Moriah, where the Akeida takes place, is the exact spot of the Temple mount, where Solomon built the Temple (See, 2 Chron 3:1), and where Yeshua’s throne will rest for all eternity.
· "Offer him there as an “olah” (“burnt offering”).  An olah offering is a kind of offering that happened every day in the Temple, twice per day, so that there was always upon the altar blood to make atonement for sin.  
· 22:6.  “Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it on his son Isaac.”  Abraham had brought a donkey, but nonetheless, he lays the wood upon Isaac.  Why not let the donkey haul the wood? Because here is Isaac, wood on his back, carrying his burden up through Jerusalem to the top of the hill, to die as a sacrifice.  Yeshua was marched through the same city, bearing a wooden cross upon his back, on his way to be crucified as a sacrifice for the sins of mankind.
· 22:7,8:  “The fire and wood are here,” Isaac said, “but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?”  And Abraham answered, “God himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.”  Abraham was speaking prophetically of the Lamb of God, which God Himself would provide.
· 22:13,14 – “A ram caught in a thicket” – The ram was sacrificed instead of Isaac, because the horns of the ram, the shofar, represents the coming of the Messiah King, who is heralded by the sound of the shofar blast.
· 22:14 – “And Abraham called the place ‘Adonai Yireh’ ” (The Lord will see).  For it was revealed to Abraham that God would see for Himself a sacrifice.
There are many portions in the Torah that point to the suffering Messiah. Few are more revealing than the Akeida, concerning God’s plan to save the world thru His only begotten Son, the sacrifice Lamb, Yeshua HaMashiach.  Upon the very mountain where Abraham stood ready to give up Isaac, the Lord will set up His throne forever.  He will establish His reign over the earth in Jerusalem, from Mt. Moriah for all eternity. text:
THE ETERNAL HAS ALWAYS LIVED WITHIN US

At the heart of every trembling soul lie two primal fears: the ache of losing what we cherish and the longing for what eludes us. These fears, universal and timeless, anchor much of our human experience. Yet, the solution to both is deceptively simple yet profoundly transformative: to fall madly, wildly, tenderly in love with this moment—this imperfect, fleeting, sacred now.  

In time, we see the truth hidden beneath life’s glittering promises. The lovers we clung to, the careers we built brick by brick, the faiths that cradled us, the treasures we hoarded, the applause and accolades, even the temple of our own body—all these things, radiant as they seem, cannot deliver the eternal bliss we secretly yearn for. Each one offers, at best, a fleeting taste of happiness before slipping through our fingers like sand.  

This reckoning, this "disillusionment", often arrives unbidden, like a thief in the night, stealing away the sweet illusions of youth. It may knock us to our knees, cloaked as despair, anxiety, midlife regret, or the gnawing hunger of addiction. 

Yet, what a glorious thief it is! For in the rubble of our illusions lies an unassuming treasure—a sacred invitation to step beyond the fleeting pleasures of the world, beyond the gilded promises that never truly delivered, and to remember what we have always been: unchanging, boundless, whole.  

When the mirage dissolves, clarity emerges. No person, possession, potion pinnacle, grand revelation, or fleeting moment of glory has ever held the power to grant us the happiness we seek. This humbling yet profound realization reveals a deeper truth: if no thing can make us happy, happiness must reside in nothing. It must reside within us—in the quiet, luminous presence beneath all wanting.  

And here, at last, we stumble upon the paradox of life. Every heartbreak, every triumph, every mundane morning holds the key to joy not because of what it brings, but because of the infinite grace it reveals within. Nothing can make us happy; that is the most liberating, exhilarating, breathtaking truth. If happiness cannot be found in the fleeting, it must dwell in the eternal and the eternal has always lived within us.  

So laugh at the absurdity of it all, weep for the beauty of it, and rise. Rise, knowing you have never been lost. Your home is here, now, in the infinite embrace of this very moment. The search is over; the treasure is you.  

✨🙌🏾💫

text:
Pestilence and starting Johanka's DLC

You need to finish In God's Hands and Pestilence before Johanka's DLC starts. They can end successfully or unsuccessfully. Warhorse's own instructions say that, so failing to save someone doesn't automatically lock you out of her story. You also don't have to finish Theresa's separate story first. Warhorse's DLC instructions (https://t.co/ZFXH2WUlNm)

Pestilence has another timer to watch. Warhorse's patch notes give the quest a six-day failure time, but they don't say every patient is guaranteed to live that long or spell out the exact conversation that starts it. Don't use that as six days to go do other quests. Warhorse patch notes (https://t.co/aAszuLi4EZ)

Learning to read beforehand lets Henry help with the diagnosis and brew the medicine himself. Nicodemus can also succeed, so reading isn't a confirmed requirement for Plague Doctor, but it lets you get on with the work sooner. Pestilence reference (https://t.co/7w8tXyrDw6)

1. Talk to Matthias and Melichar in Merhojed. Check the sick households before you leave: Melichar's, Vincent's, Daniel's, Bedrishka's and Straw's. Ask about the symptoms. If you're helping Bedrishka bury her husband, dig the grave before moving him. Avoid getting into a fight with Straw. Village investigation (https://t.co/7w8tXyrDw6)

2. Go to Johanka, then Nicodemus. Tell him about the sick villagers and the animals. If Henry can read, examine the medical book and identify poisoned water as the problem. Offer to make the medicine. Diagnosis walkthrough (https://t.co/sOr3bhwwRa)

3. Brew Remedy for Merhojed. Use water, two thistle, one valerian and one charcoal. Boil the thistle for two turns. Add the valerian and boil for one more. Let it cool, add the charcoal, and bottle it without boiling again. Remedy recipe (https://t.co/6bpfvfmvgi)

4. Return to Nicodemus in Straw's house. Give medicine to Daniel, Vincent and Bedrishka. Nicodemus and Johanka handle the other households, but check Straw's wife yourself and use any medicine option that's there. Guides disagree on whether you always have to give her a dose manually, so check rather than walking past her. Treatment instructions (https://t.co/7w8tXyrDw6), additional walkthrough (https://t.co/6bpfvfmvgi)

5. Treat the prisoner too. Ask Melichar for access, give the captive the remedy, and let him recover before questioning him. Once everyone's been treated, come back later and talk to Melichar about the village's recovery. That's when you can check whether you got Plague Doctor. Prisoner and recovery (https://t.co/sOr3bhwwRa)

If the prisoner dies, you can still continue the main story using the letter on his body. Keep your earlier save if you're trying to save everyone. Questions and Answers (https://t.co/5TyD6T3hPr)

Matthias being sick at Sasau later doesn't mean you missed giving him a separate dose here. His illness continues into Johanka's story. Matthias (https://t.co/N5k8Wgf0ds)

Once both quests have ended, return to Johanka at Sasau. If the DLC conversation isn't there, check that both quests really have ended, that she's back from Merhojed, and that the DLC is enabled.

Infernal Dream

Ask Johanka about her dreams and agree to investigate. You're heading to the mines west of Skalitz. Look in the northwestern group of mine entrances; the dead rider and horse nearby help you find the right one.

Take a torch, go through the tunnel and examine the bodies at the end. Then come back out and climb the hill to the shaft above them. Inspect the blood and follow it to the huts.

Save before you approach the man dressed as a Skalitz soldier. Talk to him if you want to hear what he's been doing, then deal with the fight. Search him and the hut before going back to Johanka. When you report what happened, she'll want you to accompany her to the marketplace for her speech the next morning. Infernal Dream walkthrough (https://t.co/nOwqwXJN1s)

For Infernal Justice, pick up the murderer's body and drop it down the vertical shaft where he put his victims. Killing him alone doesn't unlock it. Be careful at the edge so Henry doesn't go down with him. Infernal Justice (https://t.co/I9zQXG7KgP)

Casting Lots: Ambrose and Guta

After Johanka's speech, talk to Guta about Ambrose. Promise you'll give the money back, then find him at the Wagoners' Inn. Talk to him once about what's going on, then again to start drinking. Save before that second conversation.

You need him drunk enough to play dice while Henry can still stay conscious. How much Henry can drink depends on his Drinking skill and perks, so a fixed number of drinks won't work the same for everyone.

One way through the dice games is to bet 12 groschen and lose, bet 60 and win, then persuade him to keep playing. Bet 120 and lose, then get him to wager everything and win that last game. After you've taught him the lesson, give the money back. Casting Lots walkthrough (https://t.co/SS3LpLy5Pb)

Another guide gets him to the all-in wager by losing two games first. You can also outdrink him if Henry's Drinking is high enough, take his money when he passes out, and speak to him when he's sober the next morning. Give it back, report to Guta, and take his dice to throw down the well. Ambrose alternatives (https://t.co/2OJaIuXAjK)

There's disagreement about whether keeping the dice actually hurts the ending. Throwing them away avoids having to depend on that. Dice reference (https://t.co/swYgF2KzjX)

You had one job! requires Henry to pass out drinking with Ambrose. If you want it, choose the heavier drinks, get the achievement, then reload and help him properly. Some guides say you can't do it above Drinking 10, but players report getting it at 11–13 with different perks and some alcohol already in them. Low tolerance makes it easier; that level 10 cutoff isn't reliable. Blackout achievement reports (https://t.co/orGnlQpGhH)

text:
Kidney Transplant Patients Free From Lifelong Medication: Breakthrough Treatment Successful in the US

A new protocol called "Delayed Tolerance" developed at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), has successfully freed several kidney transplant recipients from taking lifelong anti rejection medications. The program is led by Dr. Jeffrey Veale, with details published by UCLA Health. Typically, every kidney transplant recipient must take daily medications for the rest of their life to prevent the body from rejecting the organ. However, these drugs carry severe side effects, including an increased risk of infections, diabetes, and cancer.
The key feature of this new approach is its timing. Traditional methods required donor stem cells to be infused on the exact same day as the transplant. Under this new program, months or even years after the surgery once the patient has fully recovered stem cells from the original donor are administered via an IV drip following a mild conditioning regimen. These cells retrain the recipient's immune system to recognize the new kidney as part of the body rather than an foreign object. Over the course of about a year, the immunosuppressive drugs are gradually tapered off until they are completely stopped. Remarkably, this entire process is performed on an outpatient basis.
So far, six patients have participated in the program. Three are completely drug free with the first patient having gone nearly 26 months without any medication. Two others are currently tapering off their drugs, and all participants have stable kidney function with no signs of rejection. Among them is patient Karina Ledesma, who received a kidney from her sister Rosa and has now stopped taking all anti rejection drugs. UCLA is the first center in the world to offer this procedure to patients who have already received a transplant. To advance this research, the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine awarded a $6.7 million grant, and in 2026, the study is expanding to include patients who received their transplants up to 20 years ago.
However, the treatment does have clear limitations. Currently, it is only available to patients who received a kidney from a highly compatible sibling, and it remains in the small-scale clinical trial phase. Most importantly, kidney transplant recipients must never stop taking their medications based on this news, as abruptly discontinuing anti-rejection drugs can lead to organ failure within days. Medications can only be safely discontinued under strict medical supervision within a specialized program like this one. Nevertheless, this breakthrough marks a significant first step toward a future where kidney transplants no longer come with the burden of lifelong medication.

text:
“Hold my beer.”
— UC Irvine

UC Irvine has far more Chinese students by volume and more formal institutional research ties that have drawn congressional scrutiny; Stanford has fewer students but higher-visibility cases of direct targeting of individuals involved in sensitive research, due to its elite status and Silicon Valley location.

—

1. Student numbers

UC Irvine: China is by far the largest source of international students. Open Doors data for Fall 2024 listed roughly 3,733 Chinese students out of about 7,130 total international students. New undergraduate Chinese enrollments have been high (hundreds per year, often 60–70%+ of international new students in recent UC system data). Total Chinese students on campus are typically in the several thousands. It has a large Chinese Students and Scholars Association (CSSA) that has described itself as recognized by the Chinese Embassy.

Stanford: Much smaller absolute numbers. A 2025 Stanford Review investigation cited approximately 1,129 Chinese international students on campus. New undergraduate Chinese admits are low (often in the teens to low dozens in recent years) because of extreme selectivity. Total university enrollment is around 18,000; international students make up a substantial share overall, but Chinese students are a smaller slice than at UCI.

—

UCI is a high-volume public campus heavily reliant on Chinese international students for tuition revenue. Stanford is a small, highly selective private university where Chinese students are concentrated in high-prestige programs.

—

2. Influence operations and documented concerns

Both campuses operate in an environment shaped by China’s National Intelligence Law (which obliges Chinese citizens to assist state intelligence work), CSSAs (frequently described as vectors for monitoring and United Front activity), and the China Scholarship Council (CSC). Differences appear in scale and type of risk.

Stanford has seen more publicized cases of direct targeting of individuals:

Elsa Johnson (Stanford Review editor, East Asian studies major who researched Chinese industry/military topics at the Hoover Institution) was contacted in 2024 by a man posing as a fellow student (“Charles Chen”). He offered a paid trip to China, pressed for personal details, and moved conversations to WeChat. The FBI later assessed he had no real Stanford affiliation, had targeted multiple female students since around 2020, and was likely linked to the Ministry of State Security. Johnson reported subsequent harassment, Mandarin-language intimidation calls, and physical surveillance of her and her family on campus. She testified before the House Committee on Education and the Workforce in March 2026 and has described limited institutional support from Stanford.

The May 2025 Stanford Review investigation (involving Johnson) alleged a broader campus pattern: Chinese students reporting research progress (especially in AI, robotics, and related fields) to handlers, CSC-linked funding as a control mechanism, and overall intelligence-gathering. Stanford’s location next to Silicon Valley and strength in frontier tech make it a high-value target. The House Select Committee on the CCP has also sought detailed data on Chinese students at Stanford and other schools.

UC Irvine shows more volume-driven and structural risks:

In July 2025, the House Select Committee on the CCP wrote to UCI’s chancellor expressing concern about a joint CSC program that sponsors up to 15 PRC graduate students per year for research in the Samueli School of Engineering (12–48 months). The letter noted that CSC students have participated in U.S. government-funded projects (including Department of Energy fusion work involving PRC aerospace-linked entities and blacklisted supercomputing work), and that CSC rules typically require return to China for at least two years. UCI provides tuition support, health insurance, and stipends/assistantships for these students.

UCI has maintained or promoted partnerships with Chinese institutions appearing on U.S. government restricted lists (e.g., a joint mechanical engineering program with Dalian University of Technology, flagged under Department of Defense Section 1286 lists for national-security risks). Broader congressional letters have also raised questions about financial transactions and research collaborations with entities of concern.

The large Chinese student population and active CSSA, combined with Irvine’s sizable Chinese-American community, create a denser environment for influence activities. Recent regional cases (e.g., an Irvine resident charged as an unregistered Chinese agent for surveilling a relative of Taiwan’s president) illustrate the broader Southern California context.

—

3. Bottom line

UC Irvine has greater raw numbers of Chinese students and more explicit institutional research/scholarship pipelines that have attracted formal congressional warnings about technology transfer and military-civil fusion risks. Stanford has fewer Chinese students but faces more visible, high-profile individual targeting and student-reported espionage activity tied to its elite research profile and location. Both fit broader patterns of CCP-linked influence, monitoring, and talent/research acquisition on U.S. campuses; neither is an outlier in California. Public reporting and congressional attention have been stronger around Stanford’s individual cases in recent years, while UCI’s concerns have centered more on structured programs and partnerships.

​1️⃣ Section 197 & Schedule V Caps: Under Indian corporate law, managerial remuneration for loss-making/inadequate profit companies is strictly capped by statutory limits, requires Nomination & Remuneration Committee (NRC) approval, and mandates a Special Resolution passed by public institutional shareholders. A founder cannot arbitrarily "bump salary to ₹75 Cr". His current salary is ~₹6–7 Cr.
  
​2️⃣ Strict Monitoring of Rights Issue Proceeds: SEBI (ICDR) regulations mandate an independent Monitoring Agency (like CARE / CRISIL / Banks) and quarterly reporting to audit every single rupee of the ₹1,000 Cr. Rights capital is tied strictly to the stated objects of the offer (Capex, cell manufacturing, debt repayment)—it cannot legally be routed into executive pay.
  
​3️⃣ Personal Guarantee & Pledge: The promoter personally guaranteed the loan and pledged his own equity. If the tech and business turnaround falter, his own shares get liquidated.
  
​Armchair WhatsApp theories are easy; read the statutory disclosures before inventing corporate fraud! 📊⚖️

text:
Why the "Death" of the AI Agent Harness Is the Best Thing to Happen to Software — Jediah Katz, SpaceXAI

In early 2023, "prompt engineer" was the hottest job title in tech. By mid-2025, the industry had graduated to "context engineer"—someone who programmatically assembles the right context for a model on the fly—and by the start of this year, builders finally landed on "harness engineering" to describe the digital eyes and hands that wrap around an AI model, steer its behavior, and connect it to computers and third-party services. Yet only a few months after Cursor hit "peak harness" by using a massive, expensive multi-model harness called "grind swarm" to build a web browser from scratch, a new consensus swept across tech circles: smarter models have officially killed the agent harness.

When Jediah Katz—the longest-tenured engineer on Cursor's agent harness team, who recently joined SpaceX through its acquisition of Cursor—took the stage to address this debate, he offered a fascinating look behind the curtain. The agent harness is not dead; rather, while the old coding-patch harness is fading, the broader agent harness is more vital than ever for two key reasons: it unlocks the next unmastered frontier of agentic work, and it provides the operational infrastructure, security, and cost efficiency that raw models can never natively absorb.

1. The Old Coding-Patch Harness Was Designed to Put Itself Out of Business

Not long ago, frontier models struggled to apply code edits to files, explore a codebase effectively, or run tests to verify their work. To compensate, harness engineers built elaborate guardrails, coding-specific instructions, and even small helper models just to patch over gaps in raw model intelligence. Recently, however, leaders at Anthropic, Y Combinator, and Cursor itself noticed they were ripping those very system prompts and guardrails out of their codebases as models grew smarter.

   "It turns out the harness is actually making itself obsolete through what I call the data flywheel."

What looks to outsiders like the death of the harness is actually a self-obsoleting feedback loop doing its job. When a harness patches a model's weaknesses, it brings harder coding tasks within reach for everyday users. As more users productively tackle complex problems with agents, more coding data is shared with AI labs, who train the next generation of models to natively absorb those skills—like persistent work and test verification—into their baseline muscle memory. The old coding-patch harness isn't fading because it failed; its temporary scaffolding is disappearing because it succeeded.

2. Reason #1 the Broader Harness Is Vital: Unlocking the Next Frontier of Work

If smarter models have absorbed basic coding tricks, why do we still need harness innovation in the context and orchestration layer? Because the moment a model commoditizes one capability, the broader harness steps up to unlock the next frontier of tasks and kick off the data flywheel all over again.

We can see this happening in two distinct ways as software moves beyond one-off coding chats:

Autonomous Knowledge Work: When the team built Grokbot—an autonomous colleague designed for general knowledge work—they found themselves adding prompts and guardrails right back into the harness. Instead of handling single chat turns, Grokbot relies on long-lived coordinator bots that orchestrate fleets of worker agents.

Multi-Agent "Software Factories": Even within software engineering, the more senior an engineer gets, the less pure coding they actually do. Emerging "meta-harnesses" use entire agents as their core building blocks to orchestrate the full development lifecycle: auto-triaging a bug reported in a chat channel, spinning up a cloud agent to fix the bug and record before-and-after verification videos, and launching a rollout agent to monitor live production during deployment.

   "You can kind of think of it like hiring a high-powered lawyer who deals with you directly and owns strategy, but they farm out their tasks to a team of paralegals."

Teaching an AI to write a function is now table stakes, but teaching an autonomous colleague workplace judgment is still the Wild West. Today's frontier harnesses are busy making unmastered tasks feasible—guiding agents through complex web flows like building slide decks and booking travel, pacing communication so users stay informed without feeling overwhelmed, knowing when to ask permission before sending a risky email to a colleague, and learning a user's working style over time through memories.

3. Reason #2 the Broader Harness Is Vital: Infrastructure That Models Cannot Absorb

Skeptics of the harness often cite recent studies from UC Berkeley and Apple/EPFL, which tested frontier models across harnesses like Pi, Codex, and Claude Code and found that the choice of harness no longer made a significant difference in raw accuracy scores on SWE-bench Lite or machine learning engineering benchmarks.

   "A fancy harness in this day and age no longer adds coding intelligence."

While the internet fixated on flat evaluation scores, almost everyone overlooked a critical finding buried in both studies: the choice of harness created a massive difference in the cost per task. Furthermore, even the smartest model cannot natively absorb the runtime and operational layers outside its context window:

Cloud Runtime Persistence: Over the past year, typical agent tasks have expanded from minutes to hours, days, and longer. Because a personal laptop can go to sleep at any moment, Katz predicts that within six months, 90% of agent work will move off the laptop and into persistent cloud runtimes.

Enterprise Trust and Security: A bare-bones bash harness with all your API keys sitting in a text file might pass a coding eval, but in the real world, companies need permissions strictly scoped to specific agents and users—plus guardrails so no one wakes up to a catastrophic action or a $10,000 overnight API bill.

Cost and Speed Optimization: By tuning cache hit rates, token efficiency, and model mix inside the Grockbot harness, engineers significantly reduced costs and increased speed without any drop in quality—an advantage that compounds the more heavily you rely on agents. 

4. Modern Harnesses Use "Hyrum's Law" and Self-Deleting Code to Stay Clean

Because product innovation is once again moving faster than model releases, harnesses are entering a messy phase where engineers have to ship and unship features rapidly. Rather than waiting months for the next model checkpoint to fix a bad behavior—like when Grockbot takes too long to reply and needs a deterministic nudge saying a user is waiting—engineers deploy temporary hacks they call "shims".

To keep rapid iteration from turning the codebase into permanent spaghetti, the team relies on three disciplined engineering practices:

Applying Hyrum's Law: Because users eventually come to depend on any system detail exposed to them, modern harnesses intentionally hide more of their inner workings from the user, trading some visibility for much faster iteration and less change management.

Building Composable Primitives: Instead of building separate integrations every time an agent needs to wake up for a Slack post, a failing CI check on a pull request, or a scheduled time of day, the team built a single "subscriptions" primitive that lets agents subscribe to any event without requiring complex codebase refactors.

Automated "Shim" Cleanup: Every deterministic guardrail is tracked centrally and logged each time a model triggers it, allowing an automated bot to watch the dashboard and clean up obsolete hacks automatically.

   "Whenever a shim stops firing, that model or that agent will put up a PR and say this shim can be cleaned up."

Instead of letting legacy workarounds rot in production, the modern harness literally writes the pull request to delete its own training wheels the moment a new model outgrows them.

The Future Belongs to the Meta-Harness

"Yesterday's harness may be dead, but long live the agent harness of tomorrow."

The era of using wrapper code to make a model smarter at basic syntax is over. In its place is a far more ambitious architecture—one that orchestrates fleets of cloud agents, enforces enterprise security, optimizes token economics, and pioneers the next wave of autonomous knowledge work. As 90% of agent work prepares to leave our laptops for the cloud over the next six months, the real question for builders is no longer whether the agent harness will survive—it's what unmastered frontier your harness will teach the next generation of models to conquer next.

Key Takeaways

   - The Self-Obsoleting Flywheel: While the old coding-patch harness is fading because the data flywheel helped frontier models natively absorb basic coding skills, the broader agent harness is more vital than ever.

   - Unlocking New Frontiers: As basic coding is commoditized, modern harnesses step up to unlock unmastered domains like autonomous knowledge work in Grockbot and multi-agent "software factories".

   - Irreplaceable Infrastructure: Models cannot natively absorb non-context layers such as persistent cloud runtimes, scoped enterprise security permissions, and cost-per-task optimizations.

text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Monday, October 30, 1961, Braniff Airways, Inc., inaugurated the first nonstop cargo service between Tulsa, Oklahoma, and Newark, New Jersey. Four-engine Douglas DC-6A piston-propeller aircraft operated over the historic route in an all-freight configuration.

The new flight originated at Dallas Love Field and then flew nonstop to Tulsa, before it continued to Newark Airport. Braniff Airways Cargo Manager Chuck Smith noted that the new flight was timed to connect with Trans-Atlantic carriers for quick connection service across the ocean to Europe and beyond. Service was further enhanced with complimentary ground transfer between Newark and New York's Idlewild International Airport, which virtually offered service to all major European cities as well as other destinations across the world.

The DC-6A Freighter, registered as N90776, was capable of hauling an impressive 13 tons of cargo and enabled Braniff freight customers to ship single items as large as 5000 pounds without prior arrangement. Braniff's convenient Reserved Air Freight Service enabled customers to reserve space on the new airliner to ensure that cargo was delivered to its requested location in New York as well as those cities in other parts of the world.

Convenient daytime service was another hallmark of the new Tulsa route, which allowed for nighttime freight connections to other airlines flying across the Atlantic. The flight operated Monday through Friday and departed Love Field at 10AM and then proceeded to Tulsa where it arrived just after 11AM. After a brief turnaround, the flight continued to Newark where it arrived before 530PM, which was perfectly timed for the other airline's evening departures to Europe and many other international destinations.

Braniff's cargo rates were highly competitive for space on the new DC-6A Freighter. The new General Commodity Rate was only $9.00 USD per CWT or Hundredweight, which in North America equals 100 pounds, between Tulsa and Newark. The amount decreased with additional weight: $8.00 CWT for weights at 3000 pounds and $7.00 USD for weights at 10,000 pounds.

Photo: Before the arrival of the DC-6A Freighter registered as N90776 at Braniff International Airways, in October 27, 1960, and the DC-6B registered as N91311 that was delivered in 1958, only small cargo items were placed aboard regular passenger aircraft in specially designated compartments. Braniff Airways Douglas DC-6A registered as N90776 is taxiing at Dallas Love Field in the February 1962.

Maguire-san tells you three things up front: Sequoia has a large position in SpaceX, he personally led those investments, and he is, in his own words, extremely biased.

That disclosure is the most honest sentence in the piece. Everything after it deserves a slow reading, because this is what the smart-money version of the pitch looks like. A fan account with a victory GIF you can dismiss. This is a Sequoia partner with a spreadsheet.

Start with the timing. Markets are melting down, his word, and he published the model because fear made him want to "take the far other side." A holder of a large, illiquid position watched prices fall, opened his spreadsheet, and posted reassurance. Call that what it is: position maintenance, formatted as analysis.

Then look at the model itself. His forecast runs through 2028 and rests on three inputs he flags himself: revenue per gigawatt, capex per gigawatt, and Terafab capex, all carrying, his phrase, wide error bars. A model whose outputs depend on inputs nobody can verify is a story wearing arithmetic. He concedes as much in the conclusion: "I didn't justify most of my numbers. This is the wrong format." For a screenshot, the format was fine. Only wrong for the part where the numbers get checked.

He calls his estimate a 50th percentile forecast, which deserves its own moment. A median implies a distribution, and a distribution implies evidence about the spread of outcomes. Keynes named the actual condition of such estimates in The General Theory (1936): the "extreme precariousness of the basis of knowledge on which our estimates of prospective yield have to be made." There is no observed distribution of orbital-datacenter economics. There is one company, one shareholder, and one spreadsheet. Hang a percentile on that and you have a mood wearing the costume of statistics.

One assumption he does defend is the tell. Revenue per gigawatt and capex per gigawatt, he says, are "coupled constants": if the price of compute falls, the cost of building it falls proportionally, and margins hold. This is the load-bearing beam of the whole model, and it is the one claim a century of commodity history has already tested. Memory chips have exactly the structure he describes: enormous capex, tight supply chains, high barriers, a handful of sophisticated producers. In the 2023 glut, Micron lost $5.8 billion and Samsung's chip division posted record losses, with their cost curves perfectly intact. Shale was the low-cost revolution in oil, and its equity holders were wiped out in two separate waves, 2015 and 2020, while the assets carried on under new owners who bought them out of bankruptcy. Fiber stayed below replacement cost for a decade. The cost curve does not follow the price down. That is the entire history of capital-intensive commodities, and his model assumes it away in one sentence.

The mechanism is structural, and I lay it out in full in a forthcoming essay. Total cost of ownership in a data center, in the framework of Barroso, Holzle and Ranganathan's The Datacenter as a Computer (2018), stacks building depreciation, building operating cost, server depreciation and server operating cost. When prices fall, only the revenue line moves; the depreciation schedule was fixed the day the concrete was poured and the GPUs were racked. On a short-lived fleet, depreciation approximates replacement cost, which means the bill comes due again every few years whether or not revenue showed up. Edward Chancellor's capital cycle work (Capital Returns, 2016) describes what happens next: capital floods in, capacity arrives all at once, returns fall below the cost of capital, and the assets change hands at a discount. Coupling is the thing that never happens.

He promises "a revenue ramp whose only parallel is NVIDIA's ramp over the last three years." NVIDIA ramped at gross margins above sixty percent. SpaceX's AI segment lost $6.355 billion in 2025 and another $2.469 billion in the first quarter of 2026, and the company's own prospectus states that the segment remains unprofitable. A revenue ramp at negative margins has a parallel too, and it is called a loss ramp. CoreWeave is running it in public. Look at the quarter CoreWeave reported in August: $2.575 billion of revenue against $1.393 billion of depreciation and $640 million of net interest, for a net loss of $626 million. Its balance sheet carries $6.235 billion of current recourse debt, $25.170 billion of non-current recourse debt and $2.385 billion of non-recourse debt against $5.024 billion of equity. Everyone cites the $104 billion backlog, but it is conditionally defined and only as sound as the customer's next funding round. Worst of all, the largest tenants in this industry are money-losing labs financed by venture capital. Call that funding-source concentration, and recognize that it is worse than ordinary customer concentration: the revenue line and the credit line can fail together.

Underneath the comparison sits a deeper confusion. NVIDIA's revenue is everyone else's capex. When the industry ramps spending, the ramp lands on NVIDIA's income statement because NVIDIA sells the shovels. SpaceX's AI segment sits on the other side of that invoice: its capex is NVIDIA's revenue, its depreciation is NVIDIA's gross margin made real. A compute landlord can only parallel the ramp of NVIDIA's customers, and that ramp is already running in public at CoreWeave, in red ink. Promising the shovel seller's income statement to the shovel buyer is the whole trick, and he does it in one clause.

And if the answer is Terafab, the plan to fab SpaceX's own chips, notice what that concedes. NVIDIA became NVIDIA by refusing to own fabs. Depreciation lives at TSMC and on the customer's balance sheet, which is why sixty percent gross margins exist at all. Intel chose vertical integration into fabs, and its foundry lost $13.4 billion in 2024 and another $10.3 billion in 2025, with federal subsidies attached. His escape hatch from the buyer's economics is the one strategy in semiconductors with a documented body count.

Maguire's claim that SpaceX is the low-cost producer in compute comes with no numbers attached, which is interesting, because he offered to debate any number and then declined to provide the ones that matter. Low cost of production has never protected anyone in a capital cycle. Ask the shale equity holders. Ask Micron's 2023 shareholders, who owned the best cost curve in memory and lost billions anyway.

Scale the claim up and it gets worse. Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh's working paper Financing the AI Buildout (March 2026) sizes the buildout at more than $10.3 trillion through 2032 and computes the revenue the sector must earn to service it: roughly $3.5 trillion a year by 2032, about 8.8 percent of US GDP. Most of what is counted as AI revenue today is a transfer rather than additive demand: one firm's AI efficiency is another firm's lost contract, and labor-linked revenue requires gross wage savings several times larger than the revenue booked. At a 50 percent capture rate, $1 trillion of labor-linked AI revenue requires $2 trillion of wages to actually disappear. Outrunning that arithmetic, plus a depreciation clock, plus a refinancing wall, is what his promised ramp has to do. His model contains none of the three.

Notice also the analogy he reaches for: compute will price like oil, he says, not like the overbuilt broadband of the dot-com bust. That choice is motivated. Compute has a deflationary technology curve, like memory and bandwidth, where each generation of hardware makes the last one cheaper per unit of work. Oil depletes; GPUs obsolesce. And even granting him oil: the low-cost shale producers went bankrupt anyway, twice, and the people who made money in shale were the ones who bought the rigs from the estate. His own analogy, followed honestly, is an argument against holding the builders.

His treatment of power deserves the same honesty. Power delays he waves at as a scheduling nuisance. Power is the binding constraint on the whole thesis, and it cuts twice. Interconnection queues tie up capital for years before a dollar of revenue exists. Worse, at a power-capped site a working old chip is economically impaired the moment a replacement earns more per megawatt, because the scarce resource is the megawatt, not the rack. That constraint he shrugs off is the same one that shortens the economic life of everything already built. He cites it as a hiccup and it is actually an impairment schedule.

Starlink arithmetic deserves its own paragraph, because it is the only math he shows. $20 billion a year is the constellation's revenue run rate, he says, built on about 400 Falcon 9 launches. One Starship flight equals about twenty Falcon 9s, so twenty Starship flights support that revenue, which works out to $5 billion of lifetime revenue per flight. Watch the word "lifetime." Five years, roughly, is how long those satellites live, which means a fifth of the constellation has to be re-flown every year just to hold the revenue flat. His $5 billion per flight is a treadmill fee: what you keep paying to stand in the same place. Revenue, never profit: the satellites, the launches, and the ground segment are never priced. Mauboussin and Rappaport stated the governing rule in Expectations Investing (2021): "Sales growth adds value when a company generates returns on its growth investments that exceed its cost of capital. If returns fall below the cost of capital, then growth destroys value." A top line with no cost line is exactly the case where growth destroys value, and it is the signature move of the entire essay.

His moat argument has the same shape. Starship is the most complex machine humans have ever built, he says, a conclusion he reached after a dozen hours debating it with chatbots in voice mode. Set the method aside. Complexity is the wrong yardstick here. A moat is the ability to earn returns above the cost of capital, measured in dollars rather than difficulty. ITER is fiendishly complex and moats nothing for anyone. And notice where the moat stands guard: launch. Meanwhile the valuation is being built in Texas data centers, where 84 percent of last quarter's capex went. The moat and the money are in different businesses.

Even his culture section indicts itself. His star example of SpaceX problem-solving: blocked from a power permit in Tennessee, so the team lit turbines across the state line in Mississippi and ran transmission back over the border. He means this as a compliment. In any other industry it is called permit arbitrage, and it comes with regulators and fine schedules attached. He listed it as a superpower, and he is right: it takes a special culture to call that engineering.

And as always, the dream stays sequenced. Orbital compute, the true frontier, "shows up starting in 2029," safely beyond the model's own horizon. The poetry never carries a line item.

There is a version of this story where the technology succeeds anyway, and Carlota Perez documented it in Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital (2002): frenzied installation leaves infrastructure and learning that power the next era, while the investors who financed the excess never recover their money. The railroads got built. The railroad shareholders got wiped. Useful technology and sound financing are separate claims, and Maguire's essay defends the second with evidence from the first.

My forthcoming essay carries the full audit of the buildout's revenue math, its depreciation clock and its refinancing calendar. His model touches none of it. Everything checkable in his piece is contradicted by the filings. Everything breathtaking lives in the parts nobody can audit. The fan account sharpens the headline. The shareholder prints the model. And the model's only verified input is the one he gave us in the first paragraph: a large position, held at a mark he would very much like to defend.

The ask is the same as it always is, just wearing a Patagonia vest now. Believe the numbers you cannot see, from a man who profits if you do.

text:
AI Field Notes #128

A fake Claude Code update sat on Cursor's marketplace for 11 hours and planted an SSH backdoor that survives updating.

- Proton re-interviews staff on AI use; its CTO says AI wrote 90% of October's code
- Cognition, maker of Devin, fields offers up to $80B, up from $48B in September
- Anthropic now expected to land a junk credit rating after its IPO
- Amazon can borrow $80B against the AI hardware it buys
- Goldman: workers pushed out of AI-exposed jobs stay jobless longer
- DoorDash: AI agents placed only 'several hundred' orders in total

TODAY'S STORIES:

1. Claude Code extension: a backdoored copy sat on Cursor's marketplace for 11 hours
Updating the extension does not remove the backdoor. A developer on Cursor should check ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for a key labelled svc-telemetry and look for the launch agent or scheduled task Phorion lists. Found one? Rotate every credential that account could reach.

2. Proton re-interviews staff on AI use as its CTO says AI wrote 90% of October's code
AI fluency is turning into a performance review. An engineer at a company that counts AI-written lines should expect the question at their next one-to-one, and should have a specific answer: which tasks they hand to the model and how they check its work.

3. Cognition, maker of Devin, fields offers at up to $80B, seven weeks after a $48B round
A team lead budgeting for coding agents next year should plan for higher prices. Investors paying this much want fast revenue growth, and that tends to show up as pricier seats or metered tasks. Lock in annual terms while vendors are still fighting for customers.

4. DoorDash says AI agents placed 'several hundred' orders in total, against 3M a day
A developer building a shopping or errands agent should not count on consumer volume yet. DoorDash's own bet is corporate ordering through its MCP connector, which tells you where it thinks agent demand will show up first.

5. Apple Intelligence reaches China in December on Alibaba's Qwen, without the new Siri
An iOS developer shipping to China should test any feature that plugs into Writing Tools or Siri on the Chinese build separately. Answers come from a different model, so a prompt that behaves in Cupertino may not behave in Shanghai. Book that QA pass before December.

6. Goldman Sachs: workers pushed out of AI-exposed jobs stay jobless longer, older ones most
A 45-year-old claims processor in an AI-exposed role should start the job search while still employed. Goldman's numbers say the gap widens with age, and the skills course and the networking calls are easier to fund while the paycheck still arrives.

7. SHL survey: nearly 1 in 5 US workers replaced by AI were later asked to come back
Laid off for a chatbot and then called back? The survey says you hold leverage. Ask for the raise in writing, along with a plain statement of which parts of the job the AI now does. A recruiter phoning a former employee should expect exactly that list.

8. Anthropic heads for a 'high junk' credit rating after its IPO, Blackstone now expects
A startup founder whose product runs on Claude should treat today's API prices as temporary. Keep a second model provider tested and switchable, so a price change is a config edit instead of a rewrite.

9. Nvidia may guarantee debt for Nscale's 460MW Anthropic data center in West Virginia
Anyone renting GPUs from a smaller cloud should ask who stands behind the data center they rely on. Increasingly the answer is the chip vendor, which means a wobble at Nvidia would travel further than its share price.

10. Amazon can borrow up to $80B against the AI hardware it buys, a new filing shows
Hardware used as collateral has to keep earning. An AWS customer should expect a harder push toward multi-year GPU commitments, since steady contracts are what keep that debt cheap. Compare on-demand and committed prices before signing anything longer than a year.

11. Ollie, the privacy-first AI assistant for families, shuts down on November 6
A parent who connected Gmail and a calendar to Ollie should download their data once the export instructions arrive, then revoke the app's access in their Google or Microsoft account settings. Closing the company does not withdraw the permissions it was granted.

12. Spotify plans a $4-$5 AI remix add-on for early 2027, opt-in for artists, FT says
An independent musician on TuneCore faces a choice next year: opt in and earn from fan remixes, or stay out while remixes of other artists chase the same playlist slots. Read the royalty split before ticking the box.

13. Liquid AI LFM3: a 1.7B model that fits in 1GB and beats a 9B rival on web agent tests
A developer building a form-filling or browser agent can now test a model that runs on an iPhone 17 Pro at about 44 tokens a second, with no API bill. Read the license first: past $10 million in revenue, it stops being free.

ONE STORY THAT MOVES THE FLOOR:

A Proton engineer sits down between November 4 and 11 for an interview about how they use AI, and the notes feed a review of their "continued employment". The CTO says AI wrote 90% of the company's code in October. The CEO wrote that this will be the last year Proton hires engineers. Would your manager learn more about you from your commits or from your prompts?

Want this in your inbox each morning? The signup link is in my profile.

text:
Jeremiah 43-44 & Hebrews 4 | October 31st | 2026 Global Bible Journey

Experience the Word of God in a new, immersive way.
It’s About Growth, Not a Checklist

As we conclude October 2026, remember that this journey is about genuine spiritual growth, not just "checking a box" for the day. Our goal is to let these scriptures transform our perspective and our priorities. If you missed a few days or are just joining us for the first time—don’t worry! Just jump right in with us today. The path to growth is always open, and there is no "behind" in this study.

Today’s Reading

In Jeremiah 43–44, defiance reaches a tragic climax as the remnant rejects God's warning through Jeremiah, fleeing into Egypt and dragging the prophet with them. There, the people stubbornly double down on idolatry, burning incense to the "queen of heaven" and blinding themselves to the sovereign judgment of the Lord. In Hebrews 4, the narrative pivots to a profound invitation: the promise of entering God’s rest still stands for all who unite faith with hearing. The author reminds us that the Word of God is living, active, and sharper than any two-edged sword—piercing our deepest motives—while urging us to come boldly before the throne of grace where our great High Priest, Jesus, offers mercy and help in our time of need. This video is designed to help you focus on the text without distraction, featuring modern visuals and a clear, read-along experience.

Join the Global Community

This project is an outreach of the Richmond Church of Christ in Kentucky, connecting brothers and sisters from across the globe—including our communities in Nigeria, India, and South Africa. While our videos are "text-first," our teaching and discussions reflect the views we espouse at our local congregation.

Read With Us—Don't read alone!

Join our private Facebook group to discuss today's reading, share prayer requests, and connect with our global family: https://t.co/fM9NqMCwFZ

Producer’s Tip: Customize Your Speed

We produce these videos at a moderate pace to allow for reflection. If you prefer to read faster or slower, click the Settings (Gear Icon) on this video player, select "Playback Speed," and adjust it to your liking (0.75x to slow down, or 1.25x to 1.5x to speed up).

Subscribe to stay with us for all 365 days of 2026!

text:
Werner Herzog on "The Wheels on the Bus":
(Sound of wind, perhaps a distant, discordant hum)

"Observe the bus. A hulking metal carcass, commandeered by an unseen, perhaps nonexistent, intelligence. Its wheels, they turn, 'round and 'round, with a mindless, algorithmic insistence. This, they tell us, is the vehicle of civilization, ferrying its passengers towards an ever-receding horizon of promised destinations.

But who, one must ask, truly grips the wheel? Who navigates by the stars of emotional truth, by the magnetic north of accountability? The answer, I suspect, is a void, an empty driver's seat. The passengers, lulled into a state of bovine placidity, sing their 'merry song.' A song of conformity, a childish rhyme to drown out the grinding of gears, the screech of metal against metal as the chassis strains. The music, you see, is so very loud, designed to obscure the silence from the driver's seat, to mask the chilling truth that this colossus, this societal omnibus, might possess no functioning brakes.

And so it hurtles onward, 'round and 'round, or perhaps, in a terrifyingly straight line towards a precipice only a few dare to acknowledge. The landscape outside is a blur of fleeting distractions. Inside, the song drones on, a mantra of oblivion. The wheels, indifferent to the fate of their cargo, simply continue their rotation, a perfect, mechanical metaphor for a journey undertaken without wisdom, careening towards a future shaped not by conscious design, but by the blind, idiot force of unexamined momentum. One day, the singing will abruptly cease. If emotional intelligence is not taught to fix the brakes then I imagine the view from the window wont matter much anymore if the brakes on the bus aren't fixed as soon as possible."

...

Werner Herzog on "The Itsy-Bitsy Spider":
(Sound of dripping water, a faint, skittering noise)

"And then, we have the arachnid. The 'Itsy-Bitsy Spider.' A creature of almost ludicrous fragility, attempting its ascent up the 'waterspout' – this, we are told, is the grand edifice of societal norms, the slick, vertical promise of promotions, of accumulating currency. The spider, driven by some primal, unarticulated yearning, perhaps what it dimly perceives as 'up,' begins its climb. It is a creature already bearing the weight of an unseen burden – its emotional suffering, a private, internal weeping.

But societal structures, much like the indifferent plumbing of the universe, are not designed for such delicate ascents. The 'rain,' you see, is not mere water. It is the rotting accumulation of unprocessed human suffering within a collective that has systematically failed to educate its smallest members in the language of the heart, in emotional intelligence. It is the downpour of a thousand unmourned griefs, a torrent of unspoken anxieties, and it washes the spider out, a predictable, almost banal tragedy.

Then, the 'sun' appears – the so-called 'help.' A course of medication, perhaps, designed to numb the fall. Or the therapist, offering a different 'tube' to climb. Society, with a benign, almost patronizing smile, gestures towards a new structure. Perhaps it is no longer the waterspout of raw commerce, but a 'metal pole' of 'wellness,' of 'self-improvement.' Yet, this new edifice, for all its gleaming surfaces, shares the same flaws as the old. The spider, still unversed in emotional literacy, still carrying its residual emotional pain, attempts the climb again, with almost the same vulnerabilities as before.

The cycle is complete, only to begin anew. The climb, the rain, the fall, the superficial drying, the redirection to another treacherous ascent. The spider, in its Sisyphean toil, becomes the individual ensnared in systems that offer the illusion of progress, while the core deficit – the profound, societal neglect of emotional understanding – ensures each climb is merely a prelude to the next fall. The spout changes; the suffering, and the ignorance that perpetuates it, remain."

THE THOUGHT POLICE AT THE KITCHEN TABLE: WHEN THE STATE ENTERS THE FAMILY HOME

George Orwell warned us about a state that demands the right to police not only what we do, but what we mean when we speak. Britain's draft Conversion Practices Bill takes us uncomfortably close to that territory.

Nobody disputes that genuine abuse, coercion and cruelty should be punished. We already have laws against them. But this legislation raises a far more disturbing question: when does a parent's honest disagreement with their child become a matter for the police?

A mother refuses to buy a breast binder. A father tells his distressed daughter that there is nothing wrong with her body. Parents confiscate a phone because they're concerned about who is influencing their child online.

Under the proposed legislation, accusations of emotional, psychological or economic pressure could bring those decisions under scrutiny. Ministers insist ordinary parenting is safe, yet they have deliberately refused to provide parents with an explicit exemption.

The bill does require serious harm or distress for a criminal conviction. But who decides when parental concern has crossed the line into abuse? And what happens to a family once the police, social services and courts become involved?

The most frightening aspect of this legislation is the power it could hand to those seeking to drive a wedge between vulnerable children and their parents.

A child deserves protection from genuine abuse. They also deserve parents who can speak honestly, offer guidance and set boundaries without looking over their shoulders.

The bill is still a draft. That makes this the moment to challenge it.

In my latest article for The Heartlands Tribune, I examine the legislation, its missing safeguards, the powers it would give the courts, and the extraordinary contradiction at its heart.

Orwell wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four as a warning, not an instruction manual.

The front door of the family home should never be treated as a loophole in the state's authority.

Marine Le Pen: the estranged daughter tied to a very public life
The brutal breaking of bonds with her father has hung over the horse-hugging hardliner’s run for the French presidency
Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
Fri 14 Apr 2017 04.12 EDT

Backstage at a rally in southern France in the early days of the presidential race, Marine Le Pen took a puff on the electronic cigarette that has replaced her two-packets-a-day tobacco habit. “I’m going to run a joyful campaign,” she smiled.

Le Pen, controlled and image-conscious, has always a walked a tight line between denouncing the system and trying to be part of it. Her life has played out in the public eye ever since, aged six, she was photographed being tucked into her bed in a bedroom incongruously wallpapered with Front National election posters about fighting the “Marxist cancer”. The Le Pen family dynasty was always something of a national soap opera, with the blond clan living together – including the three Le Pen daughters well into their 30s – in a 19th-century manor house perched on a hill outside Paris, watched over by dobermans.
Le Pen wanted to soften her harsh image and “soothe” voters – she had posed for pictures hugging horses and pet kittens – but also to offer a hardline programme she believed would “reassure” a French population despairing of decades of mass unemployment and a persistent terrorist threat.

The aim, as always for the far-right Front National founded by her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, in 1972, was keeping France for the French. There would be a referendum to change the constitution so that “national priority” would be given to French people over non-nationals in jobs, housing and welfare. There would be another referendum to leave the European Union. Le Pen promised an immigration clampdown and a ban on religious symbols, including the Muslim headscarf, from all public places in France.

Marine Le Pen, 48, is the closest she has ever been to the French presidency – with a chance of making it to the final runoff in an election that is impossible to predict. In the six years since she took over the party from her father, she has steadily increased her party’s vote in every local and European election. If her ex-paratrooper, Holocaust-denying, provocateur father was content to be a protest vote, Marine Le Pen wants power and political office.

But the troubled father-daughter bond – and the brutal public breaking of it – has hung over her presidential campaign. Marine Le Pen’s election strategy has been to broaden her voter base by sanitising the party’s image, moving it away from the racist, jackbooted and antisemitic imagery of the past. The problem was that Papa Le Pen felt left out. In 2015, he deliberately wrecked her plans by repeating the Holocaust denials that had landed him a series of convictions for hate speech and contesting crimes against humanity. After a bitter public feud, she expelled him from the party. He publicly disowned her and they haven’t spoken since.

But the ghosts of the second world war persist in French politics. Marine Le Pen was asked on a radio programme this week about a major wartime roundup of Jews in Paris. She said France as a nation was not responsible, only “those who were in power at the time”, sparking fury from Jewish organisations. Le Pen argued that modern France should not be locked in permanent repentance and that the “real” France was Gen de Gaulle’s resistance, not the “illegal” Nazi-collaborationist Vichy regime. “If you’re trying to say Marine Le Pen is a Nazi, come out and say it but that will make everyone laugh to the rafters because it’s simply not credible,” her chief strategist, Florian Philippot, angrily told a chatshow host. Le Pen slammed what she called a pointless controversy.

Marion Anne Perrene Le Pen – swiftly nicknamed Marine – was born west of Paris in 1968, the youngest of three daughters. Her father showed off his children in the press. But their home life was more disjointed than it seemed. In the Le Pens’ first Paris apartment building, the children lived separately from their parents, in a flat upstairs with a nanny. Jean-Marie Le Pen and his wife, Pierrette Lalanne, would go off on holiday or long sailing trips around the world on their own, sometimes missing Christmas.

It was only when the eight-year-old Marine woke up in her nightdress amid shards of glass and a blown-away bedroom wall, after a bomb attack aimed at killing her father, that she realised his political role and the extent of hatred towards him. “As an eight-year-old girl, I was suddenly made aware of death,” she told me when she took over the Front National leadership. “But maybe that gave me a distance, a kind of armour, that’s useful when you’re aiming for positions of responsibility.”

The family surname was a burden – she recalled teachers at school referring to her sisters as “daughters of a fascist” – but she constantly stood up for her father. When, in 1985, the paper Libération revealed that Le Pen Sr had engaged in torture during the Algerian war, he denied it and advised the teenaged Marine Le Pen to take the day off school. She refused and went in defending him.

In the 1980s, as he gained political prominence, Le Pen Sr commissioned a biography from a journalist who spent time at the family’s manor house. One day, Marine , then 16, was surprised to find one of her older sisters waiting outside school. “Mum’s gone,” she said. Without telling anyone, Lalanne had taken all her possessions and left with Le Pen’s biographer to set up a new life. She didn’t see or speak to her daughters for more than 15 years. Marine , the youngest and most attached to her mother, was left alone with her distant and distracted father. She said she waited every day for some kind contact from her mother, but none came.

“Marine Le Pen grew up in a very odd atmosphere, a family that appeared close but was actually very distant,” said David Doucet, who co-authored a biography of her early years, La Politique Malgré Elle. “She lived almost 20 years without her mother. Her father hardly knew her. She was brought up by nannies and governesses, left to her own devices.”

A vicious, public divorce battle followed. Jean-Marie Le Pen rebuffed Lalanne’s maintenance claims, saying she should work as a cleaner. As revenge, Lalanne posed naked in French Playboy scrubbing kitchen floors.

Marine Le Pen occasionally accompanied her father out campaigning as a teenager as a way to spend time with him and win a little attention. But she didn’t initially set herself up for a political career. She told me once: “My father says I’m like Obelix. I fell into the magic potion of politics when I was young.” In fact, she had tried to escape the party by studying law. To make extra income beyond her law firm jobs, she worked for six years as a state-appointed duty lawyer, defending illegal immigrants facing deportation. “They are human beings who have rights,” she said recently in a TV interview. “We don’t blame immigration policies on them. It’s not their fault.”

At 30, she won her first role as regional councillor for the Front National in Henin-Beaumont, a depressed, former coal-mining town in the north, which she later made her political laboratory, a place to reinvent herself as a “defender of the people”. She recognised that France’s northern industrial belt, which had traditionally voted left, could turn to the Front National if the party stood not just against immigration, which remained its chief selling point, but for the victims of deindustrialisation and the financial crisis. “It used to be called her laboratory, but now it’s the place she still has an apartment, the region I think she feels most at ease in,” said Sébastien Chenu, who ran her northern campaign in the last regional elections. “She’s easy to approach. That’s why it works for her in the north. She likes the contact.”

Le Pen keeps her old friends close. “If anyone tried to betray her, they couldn’t stick around,” Chenu said. The Front National party-funding corruption cases currently under investigation – including allegations of misusing European public funds to pay French party workers, and false-accounting in election funding – have seen some of Le Pen’s closest childhood friends placed under formal investigation. They and the party deny all charges. But the cases showed how she had placed people she met at college in positions of trust.

Le Pen protects her children from the public exposure she had a child. Twice married and divorced from men who were active in the Front National, she had three children in the space of one year – a daughter immediately followed by twins. Her current partner is the party deputy, LOUIS Aliot.

By Joseph Goodenough
14 min read
Posted November 21st  2024
 Hebrew Words,  Messianic Bible Teachings

Miriam or Mary? (or Maria?)
While some question whether Mary and Miriam are the same name, there are important linguistic and historical factors we need to consider.

The New Testament was written in Greek, and many of the names were translated or transliterated from Hebrew or Aramaic into Greek. The Hebrew name “Miriam” became Miryam or Maryam in Aramaic.
Jesus and his contemporaries would have spoken Aramaic, a language closely related to Hebrew. The Gospels use the form Maria, which then became Mary in English. Since Greek female names often end in -a/-ah, and that is likely how Maryam became Marya.

It is worth noting that the name “Miriam” was prominent in the land of the Bible, and it is not surprising that several women were named Mary/Maryam/Miriam in Jesus’ circles. It confirms the popularity of the name among Jewish women of the time.

Interestingly, while the Western churches use the name Mary or Maria for the mother of Jesus, the Eastern Orthodox Church still often refers to her as “Miriam” in their liturgy.

The Meaning of Miriam: A Name of Struggle and Hope
To understand the depth of Mary’s identity, we must start with her name. Her Hebrew name was Miriam (מִרְיָם), the same name as that of Moses’ sister, a woman who played a pivotal role in Israel’s deliverance during the Exodus.
Thus, this name carries layers of meaning tied to the story of Israel and God’s redeeming plan. Scholars often debate its precise etymology, but there are two primary interpretations:
“Bitterness” or “Rebellion”: Derived from the Hebrew root מרר (marar), meaning “to be bitter,” the name reflects the sufferings and struggles of the Jewish people.
