text:
Then he said something that really stayed with her.

“I thought we were both just having a good time. I didn’t know you expected a whole morning together.”

She told him she wasn’t expecting a romantic breakfast, flowers, or a relationship announcement.

She simply expected the same consideration he had shown her the night before.

He had spent hours making sure she felt wanted, comfortable, and welcome.

But when his own plans became the priority, he couldn’t even be bothered to have a proper conversation with her.

He finally offered to drive her home, but by then she had already ordered an Uber.

Before leaving, she picked up her handbag and said:

“I think what you’re missing is that I wasn’t expecting you to spend the entire morning entertaining me. I just didn’t want to feel like someone whose presence became inconvenient as soon as the night was over.”

He told her she was being unfair.

According to him, he had done nothing wrong. He invited her over, they had a good night, and he had simply continued with his personal plans.

Later that afternoon, he sent her a message.

“Hope you got home safely. I had a really good time with you last night.”

She replied:

“I did. I just think we have different ideas about consideration.”

He called her shortly afterward, saying she was allowing one awkward morning to ruin something that had been going well.

But she told my friend something interesting when we discussed it.

She said she wasn’t looking for a man who would wake up every morning and treat her like a princess.

She was looking for someone who understood that inviting another person into your private space came with a little responsibility.

And that was what bothered her.

He had been thoughtful enough to plan the entire evening, but apparently not thoughtful enough to consider the person he had invited into it.

Now, some of our friends think she’s overreacting because he never promised her a relationship or a romantic morning.

Others think he was inconsiderate, especially because he had actively persuaded her to stay.

So, is she expecting too much from a man she has only been dating for six weeks, or is basic consideration supposed to exist even when a relationship is still casual?

text:
𝗢𝗻 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗱𝗮𝘆-𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘀, 𝘄𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘂𝗽—𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻 𝗻𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗮𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗻𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁
The Peace of Wild Things
When despair for the world grows in me
and I wake in the night at the least sound
in fear of what my life and my children’s lives might be,
I go and lie down where the wood drake
rests in his beauty on the water, and the great heron feeds.
I come into the peace of wild things
who do not tax their lives with forethought
of grief. I come into the presence of still water.
And I feel above me the day-blind stars
waiting with their light. For a time
I rest in the grace of the world, and am free. “Wendell Berry”

There is something achingly tender about this poem's movement from the anxieties of the human world into the quiet embrace of the natural one. We are creatures burdened by anticipation, forever reaching into an uncertain future, grieving possibilities that have not yet come to pass. And yet, beyond the restless theatre of our thoughts, life continues in its own untroubled rhythm: the wood drake resting in his beauty, the heron feeding, the stillness of water, the stars keeping their light.

In a sense, the wild things offer us more than refuge; they remind us of a way of being we have somehow forgotten. They inhabit the present without resisting it, without carrying the imagined weight of tomorrow. Their beauty is neither performed nor intended, but simply is.

And there is something almost poignant about the stars waiting with their light. They return night after night, on this date, with the anticipation of being seen, bringing their beauty and radiance, waiting only for us, who so often never show up. We are elsewhere, absorbed in our worries, our plans, and our fears about a future that has yet to arrive. And still, they return, patiently offering their light. There is something almost like longing in this image, as though the stars, in all their quiet faithfulness, wishes to be seen, to reveal themselves, and to establish a connection with us. It reminds me of the idea that creation is a manifestation of something greater, something that wishes to be known.

This is also the mystery of grace: a gift freely given, independent of our deserving, patiently offered even when we are too distracted to receive it. The natural world makes no promises about tomorrow, nor does it ask us to abandon our fears. It simply opens before us, in all its quiet magnificence, reminding us that we belong to something immeasurably larger than our anxieties.

And, in the end, freedom is not always about finding answers or gaining control over the future. Sometimes it is simply about showing up, looking again, and allowing ourselves to be found by the grace that has been waiting for us all along.

text:
Cicero, from the 2nd Philippics.  An appropriate time of year to imbibe.  Post Inspired by @bradleybirzer 

Look  back at last, I beg you, Marcus Antonius, to the Republic.  Think of the men you are descended from, not the men you live with.  Deal with me however you like, but make your peace with the Republic.  What you do about yourself is your business; I will declare what I will do.  I defended the Republic as a young man; I will not abandon it as an old one.  I despised the swords of Catiline; I will not recoil before yours.  No, I will rather cheerfully expose my own person, if the liberty of the city can be restored by my death.  In fact I would gladly offer my body, if my death could buy back the city's freedom at once, so that the anguish of the Roman people might at last give birth to what it has so long been labouring with.
Nearly twenty years ago, in this very temple, I said that death could not come too soon to a man who had been consul.  How much more truly will I say it now of an old man?  For me, senators, death is now even something to wish for, since I have done all that I set out to achieve and have accomplished.

I wish for only two things.  First, that when I die I leave the Roman people free; the immortal gods can give me nothing greater.  Second, that each man's fortune turn out as his service to the Republic deserves.

text:
Why We Will Defend Freedom and Democracy

A Century of Authoritarianism: Lessons History Cannot Allow Us to Forget

1/7 — A Century of Political Persecution

Over the past century, authoritarian regimes have repeatedly promised national greatness, equality, or social justice.

Yet many have created systems of political imprisonment, persecution, and state violence.

History teaches us that noble promises cannot justify unlimited political power.

2/7 — Racial Struggle and Class Struggle

Hitler’s Nazism promoted racial supremacy. Mussolini’s Fascism elevated the nation and state above individual liberty.

Marxist-Leninist regimes, meanwhile, claimed to govern in the name of the working class.

These ideologies were different, but their authoritarian governments shared a dangerous practice: identifying groups of people as enemies of the state.

3/7 — The Human Cost of Dictatorship

Nazi Germany established concentration camps and carried out the Holocaust.

Stalin’s Soviet Union experienced the Great Purge, mass imprisonment, and political terror.

Mao Zedong’s Cultural Revolution brought widespread persecution, violence, and social destruction.

North Korea continues to demonstrate the dangers of hereditary totalitarian rule.

When political power becomes absolute, individual rights become vulnerable.

4/7 — China’s Economic Reforms

China’s economic transformation after 1978 offers another important lesson.

Under Deng Xiaoping, China gradually moved away from rigid central planning, expanded market mechanisms, encouraged private enterprise, and opened itself to international trade.

Millions of ordinary citizens gained greater opportunities to work, produce, trade, and build businesses.

China’s achievements demonstrate the economic importance of initiative, competition, and greater freedom of economic choice.

However, economic liberalization did not establish constitutional democracy, independent courts, or genuine multiparty political competition.

5/7 — Xinjiang and the Continuing Danger

Political persecution is not merely a historical tragedy.

Human rights organizations continue to document arbitrary detention, unjust imprisonment, mass surveillance, and restrictions on religious and cultural freedom in Xinjiang.

These abuses demonstrate the danger of political systems that lack independent judicial oversight and meaningful accountability.

No government should possess unlimited authority to imprison people because of their identity, beliefs, or peaceful expression.

6/7 — What America Must Protect

America must learn from the disasters of authoritarian rule, whether justified through racial nationalism, revolutionary class struggle, or other claims of absolute political authority.

The essential distinction is not simply between capitalism and socialism.

It is between government constrained by constitutional rights and government that places itself above those rights.

America’s constitutional republic rests on separation of powers, checks and balances, free elections, independent courts, freedom of speech, religious liberty, and equal protection under the law.

Economic reform and social justice must never become excuses for dismantling these protections.

7/7 — Our Commitment to Freedom

We believe that human dignity is greater than political ideology.

Government exists to protect the rights of the people, not to make the people servants of the state.

We can pursue economic opportunity, social justice, and national progress without sacrificing constitutional liberty.

We will defend America’s democratic foundations.

We will never accept authoritarianism as the price of prosperity.

Government of the people, by the people, for the people.

We construct a new civilization beyond ideology.

Freedom. Democracy. Human Dignity.
                                    Yankee
                        October 31 2026

text:
Bihar Has Been Discovered. Now It Must Become a Destination. There are moments when a place receives an opportunity that extends well beyond the achievement itself. Bihar may be experiencing one of those moments.

The Bihar Museum has been ranked 9th in the world & first in Asia in Worth a Journey's 2026 list of the world's 100 best museums, ahead of several internationally renowned institutions. For a state whose civilisational contribution to humanity is considerably greater than its contemporary international profile, this is an important recognition.

But the real question is not where Bihar Museum stands in a global ranking. It is what Bihar intends to do with that recognition.

Bihar has an extraordinary concentration of history, philosophy, religion, architecture & cultural heritage. Nalanda, Bodh Gaya, Vaishali, Rajgir, Pawapuri & Vikramshila represent ideas & traditions that shaped human civilisation. Nalanda & the Mahabodhi Temple are already @UNESCO World Heritage sites.

Bihar does not lack attractions. It lacks the infrastructure, organisation & international positioning to turn them into a coherent tourism experience.

France offers an interesting lesson. Its tourism economy was not built around the @MuseeLouvre or @LaTourEiffel alone. It developed an ecosystem of museums, historic towns, hospitality, transport, food & cultural experiences. Bihar should study that model, not imitate it. It needs its own tourism identity rooted in its civilisational heritage.

Patna could become the principal cultural gateway. Bodh Gaya could be strengthened as an international Buddhist destination, while Nalanda & Rajgir could develop into a combined heritage, education & wellness circuit. Vaishali, Pawapuri & Vikramshila deserve similar integration.

But announcing tourism circuits is the easy part. Making them work is the real challenge.

Bihar needs better intra state roads, reliable public transport, clear signage, clean wayside facilities & predictable travel times. It needs hotels across price categories, motels, boutique heritage properties and professionally managed homestays.

There is considerable scope for local enterprise through Madhubani art galleries, handicraft stores, regional cuisine, souvenir shops & guided cultural experiences. Clean public toilets, drinking water, waste management & well maintained public spaces must become non negotiable standards.

Patna itself needs a serious urban renewal vision. Its riverfront, historic neighbourhoods, public spaces & cultural institutions should become part of the tourism experience.

Equally important is law & order. Visitors must feel safe travelling between destinations and exploring independently. Tourist policing, responsive emergency services & strict enforcement against harassment & exploitation are essential.

The government need not build every hotel, restaurant or visitor facility. It must create a predictable investment environment, simplify approvals, strengthen infrastructure & invite credible domestic & international hospitality operators. PPP can accelerate this transformation.

Bihar must also market itself internationally, particularly across Southeast Asia, Japan, South Korea & Europe, engaging Buddhist communities, universities, cultural institutions and global travel operators.

Tourism success should not be measured merely by visitor numbers. Length of stay, visitor spending, employment generation & local business participation matter equally.

The Bihar Museum's recognition is an international endorsement. But rankings are temporary; destinations are built to last.

Bihar has the history, heritage & cultural significance. What it needs now is the institutional ambition to connect these assets through infrastructure, investment and governance.

The world has been given another reason to look towards Bihar. The state must now give the world reasons to come, stay, explore and return. https://t.co/m5of9yKe0h

Prayer is an invocation or act that seeks to activate a rapport with a deity, spirit, or object of worship through deliberate communication. By its own definition, prayer is worship.

The Bible shows it the same way. The woman of Canaan worshipped Jesus, saying, Lord, help me. Abraham's servant bowed his head and worshipped the LORD, then prayed. David asked for his prayer to be set before God as incense, the way the priests offered worship in the temple. In heaven, the prayers of saints are offered up before the Lamb like incense.

Jesus said worship God, and Him only. So when you pray to Mary, you are giving her worship that belongs only to God.

Matthew 15:25 (KJV) Then came she and worshipped him, saying, Lord, help me.

Genesis 24:26-27 (KJV) And the man bowed down his head, and worshipped the LORD. And he said, Blessed be the LORD God of my master Abraham, who hath not left destitute my master of his mercy and his truth: I being in the way, the LORD led me to the house of my master's brethren.

Psalm 141:2 (KJV) Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.

text:
Yes — the closest real science is in vitro gametogenesis, or IVG.
Researchers take a skin or blood cell, reprogram it into an induced pluripotent stem cell, then coax that cell toward becoming an egg precursor. In mice, that pipeline has produced live, fertile offspring — that was demonstrated back in twenty sixteen by Katsuhiko Hayashi’s group in Japan. In humans, nobody has gotten that far. Two separate approaches are closest right now. One is from a company called Conception, which in June of this year reported generating early-stage human egg cells — primary oocytes — from blood-derived stem cells grown into miniature ovary-like structures. Those eggs are immature and can’t be fertilized yet. The other is from Shoukhrat Mitalipov’s lab at Oregon Health and Science University, published in Nature Communications in September twenty twenty-five. They skipped the stem-cell route entirely and used somatic cell nuclear transfer — the Dolly-the-sheep method — inserting a skin-cell nucleus into a donor egg stripped of its own DNA, then inducing a division process they named mitomeiosis to halve the chromosome count. That produced eighty-two eggs. They fertilized them with sperm. Nine percent reached the blastocyst stage, but every embryo carried chromosomal abnormalities, and no pregnancy was attempted. Mitalipov’s own quote was that it “kind of partially works, and partially doesn’t.” As of today, IVG is not offered at any fertility clinic anywhere in the world. Scientists estimate at least another decade before it could be considered safe for clinical trials, and in the US a congressional rider currently blocks the FDA from even reviewing requests to start pregnancies from genetically manipulated embryos. Japan, by contrast, explicitly permitted stem-cell-derived gamete embryo research for lab purposes in July twenty twenty-five. The one thing worth separating clearly: this is not copying an existing egg. It’s building a new one from the person’s own DNA, which is both the promise and the ethical flashpoint.

text:
Dacoity. That is the word two Supreme Court judges used on 27 October for steep hospital markups.

The bench was hearing a petition seeking stricter price controls on medicines and medical consumables. A lawyer for private hospitals warned that forced margin cuts could make hospitals collapse. The bench said hospitals could survive by other means, "Not through this dacoity." The Court has reserved its order.

So how can a patient spot a markup on a bill? I built https://t.co/jCkw8RH7wD and have added a consumables page. Pick an item, type the billed amount, and see what Rajasthan pays in bulk, before GST.

A 5 ml syringe with needle costs that state ₹1.29.

Private hospitals usually pay more than a state buying in bulk, so the gap is not proof of overcharging. The Court has not adopted this list.

Until the Court rules, the page offers one fixed point: what a state pays for the same item.

text:
Every year, approximately 40,000 students enter Sri Lanka's state universities through the Advanced Level examination, one of the most brutally competitive selection processes in South Asia. They do so having survived a system that accommodates roughly 2% of those who sit the exam, having beaten odds that would be considered unconscionable in any functioning education system, and having earned, through years of relentless work in under-resourced schools with outdated syllabi and overworked teachers, the right to enter institutions that were supposed to transform their lives. What awaits them is not transformation. What awaits them is the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna.

Not in name, of course. The JVP does not hang its banner above the university gates. It does not distribute membership cards at orientation. It operates, as it has always operated, through front organisations, cadre structures, and an apparatus of control so deeply embedded in the institutional fabric of the state university system that most students cannot distinguish between the university itself and the political machine that has colonised it. The primary instrument is the Inter University Students' Federation (IUSF), an organisation that presents itself as a student advocacy body while functioning as the JVP's campus recruitment arm. The IUSF does not merely participate in university politics; it dominates them. It controls student unions. It organises protests. It enforces strikes. It determines, through a combination of ideological pressure and social coercion, what students think, what students say, what students are permitted to aspire to, and, most critically, what students are taught to blame for the fact that their lives are difficult. The answer, delivered with the consistency of liturgy, is this: you suffer because rich men drive luxury vehicles.

This is not a caricature; it is the operational thesis of an ideological programme that has been running, with remarkably little variation, for over four decades. It is delivered in orientation sessions that are not orientations but political re-education. It is reinforced through ragging rituals that are not hazing but systematic psychological reprogramming. It is embedded in the slogans painted on hostel walls, chanted at demonstrations, repeated in student council meetings, and absorbed, through sheer repetition and social pressure, into the worldview of tens of thousands of young people who entered the university capable of complex thought and leave it capable only of resentment.

The formula is simple: Sri Lanka is poor. You are poor. You are poor because wealth has been stolen from you. The people who stole it drive SUVs, live in Colombo 7, send their children to international schools, and speak in English.They are the comprador bourgeoisie, the agents of imperialism, the class enemy. Every problem you have ever experienced (the overcrowded bus you rode to school, the textbook you could not afford, the tuition class your parents sacrificed to pay for, the job that does not exist for you upon graduation) is a direct and deliberate consequence of their wealth. Their BMW is built from your poverty. Their swimming pool is filled with your sweat.

The student, fresh from Anuradhapura, Monaragala, or Polonnaruwa, nineteen or twenty years old, separated from family for the first time, exhausted from the examination, anxious about the future, and now surrounded by senior students who speak with the absolute certainty of the ideologically possessed, does not have the tools to resist this. The formula is emotionally satisfying in the way that all conspiratorial thinking is emotionally satisfying: it provides a complete explanation for suffering, identifies a visible enemy, and absolves the believer of any responsibility for their own condition. You are not struggling because the economy is structurally broken, because successive governments failed to diversify exports, because the education system prioritises rote memorisation over critical thinking, because the curriculum has not been meaningfully updated since the 1970s, because the country borrowed beyond its means, or because the state university system itself has been hollowed out by the very political forces that now claim to defend it. You are struggling because a man in Rajagiriya drives a Land Cruiser.

And the mechanism by which this idea is installed in a young person's mind is not persuasion; it is ragging. Ragging in Sri Lankan universities is not the boisterous, occasionally cruel initiation ritual familiar to universities worldwide. It is a structured, systematic programme of psychological subjugation that operates with the explicit purpose of breaking the incoming student's individual identity and replacing it with collective obedience to the senior students who control the hostel, the faculty, and ultimately the student union (which is controlled by the IUSF, which is in turn controlled by the JVP).

First-year students are forced to stand in lines at midnight. They are screamed at. They are humiliated. They are made to perform degrading tasks. They are forbidden from speaking in English, because English is the language of the class enemy, the language of the comprador bourgeoisie, the language of the people who drive luxury vehicles. They are forbidden from dressing in ways that suggest aspiration, because aspiration is bourgeois. They are forbidden from associating with students outside approved social circles. They are told, in terms that are anything but subtle, that the senior students are their protectors, their guides, and their political educators, and that the price of protection is compliance.

A student who resists is not merely excluded. A student who resists is targeted, socially isolated, and labelled a sell-out, a capitalist sympathiser, or an agent of the establishment. In a residential university where the hostel constitutes the entirety of one's social world, this is not a minor inconvenience; it is a sentence of complete social death. And students, being human, young, far from home, and desperate to belong, comply. They comply not because they believe the ideology, at least not initially, but because the cost of refusal is unbearable. Then, after months of immersion, after hearing the same slogans repeated with the same fervour by the same people in the same closed environment, something shifts. They begin to believe it, not because it is true, but because belief is the price of belonging.

Consider what this programme produces. A student enters the University of Kelaniya to study management. She is from Kurunegala. Her parents are schoolteachers. She scored high enough on the examination to qualify for a degree that should, in a functioning system, lead to employment in banking or consulting, the kind of career that would lift her family from the lower middle class into something resembling economic security.

Within her first semester, she has learned the following: the private sector is the enemy, corporations are instruments of exploitation, profit is theft, the International Monetary Fund is an agent of Western imperialism, privatisation is a conspiracy to rob the people of their birthright, English is the language of the oppressor, aspiration is collaboration, the stock market is a rigged casino for the elite, and entrepreneurship is a euphemism for exploitation.

She has not learned accounting software. She has not learned data analysis. She has not learned business communication.She has not learned any of the practical skills that would make her employable in the economy that actually exists, as opposed to the economy that the JVP claims exists: an economy in which the only meaningful distinction is between the virtuous poor and the predatory rich, and in which the only appropriate response to inequality is not personal advancement but collective struggle against the class enemy.

She graduates three years later, or four, or five, because strikes called by the IUSF have extended her degree by semesters she cannot afford to lose. She holds a degree in management from a state university, yet she cannot write a professional email in English. She has never used an enterprise software system. She has never completed an internship, because internships are in the private sector and the private sector is the enemy. She possesses a political vocabulary that would impress a 1970s Marxist theoretician and a professional skill set that would disqualify her from an entry-level position at a mid-sized firm in Colombo. She is 26. She is unemployable. And she has been taught, with absolute conviction, that this is not her fault, not the university's fault, and not the fault of the political movement that called the strikes that delayed her degree and promoted the ideology that prevented her from acquiring marketable skills. It is the fault of the man in the SUV. Multiply her by forty thousand. Multiply her by thirty years.

The genius of the operation, if one can use such a word for something so destructive, is that it is self-reinforcing. The student who graduates without employable skills cannot find work. The student who cannot find work becomes angry.The angry graduate looks for an explanation. The JVP provides that explanation: the system is rigged, the rich have stolen your future, the private sector is a closed shop for the English-speaking elite, and the only solution is political struggle.

The graduate, who has no other framework for understanding their situation because the JVP spent four years ensuring they would have no other framework, returns to the party: joins its affiliated trade unions, participates in its campaigns,votes for its candidates, and eventually sends their own children into the same state university system where the cycle repeats. The JVP did not merely indoctrinate students; it created a closed epistemological loop in which the consequences of indoctrination are interpreted through the very ideology that caused them, making escape functionally impossible without an act of individual intellectual rebellion that the system is specifically designed to prevent.

A student who begins to question (who perhaps notices that graduates of private institutions are securing jobs, or who suspects that learning English and acquiring technical skills might be more useful than attending protest marches) faces an immediate problem: the ideology has an answer for that, too. Private institutions are instruments of class reproduction. International school graduates are beneficiaries of inherited privilege. The jobs they secure are not earned, but allocated by a system designed to exclude the working class. To learn English is to collaborate with the oppressor. To acquire marketable skills is to submit to the logic of capitalism. To aspire to individual success is to betray the collective. Every exit from the loop has been pre-labelled as treason. And so, the student stays.

The JVP's opposition to private universities is perhaps the most revealing expression of this entire apparatus. For decades,successive governments have proposed establishing private universities to expand access to higher education. The numbers are damning: of the approximately 300,000 students who sit the A/L examination each year, fewer than 40,000 gain admission. The remaining 260,000 are simply abandoned by the system. They receive no tertiary education from the state. Their options are limited to poorly regulated private institutes, technical colleges with inadequate resources, or immediate entry into a labour market for which they are underprepared.

Private universities would absorb some of these students, offer alternative pathways, and create competition that might force state universities to improve. The JVP has opposed this with the ferocity of an organisation defending not a principle, but a monopoly. The stated reason is that private universities would commercialise education, creating a two-tier system in which the wealthy buy degrees while the poor are relegated to underfunded state institutions. This argument possesses a superficial plausibility that evaporates upon contact with reality.

The two-tier system already exists; it has existed for decades. The children of the wealthy already attend private universities abroad in Australia, the United Kingdom, Malaysia, and India. The JVP's opposition to domestic private universities does not prevent the rich from accessing private education; it prevents the middle class and the aspiring poor from accessing it. The son of a Colombo businessman will study in Melbourne regardless of what the IUSF thinks. It is the daughter of a Ratnapura shopkeeper, the one who scored well on the examination but not well enough for state university admission, who is left with nothing.

The JVP knows this. Tilvin Silva knows this. The IUSF leadership knows this. They oppose private universities not because privatisation would harm students, but because it would break their monopoly. If students had alternatives (environments where ragging is not tolerated, where English is taught rather than prohibited, where curricula reflect the actual demands of the real economy, and where political indoctrination is not an unofficial core module), the JVP's entire campus apparatus would collapse. The recruitment pipeline would dry up. The ideological assembly line that has produced loyal cadres for four decades would shut down. The opposition to private universities is not a principled policy position; it is an act of institutional self-preservation disguised as social justice. It has cost a quarter of a million young people each year their shot at tertiary education, solely so the JVP can continue to control the 40,000 who gain admission.

There is a particular cruelty in the party's treatment of the English language that deserves its own accounting. English, in Sri Lanka, is not merely a language; it is a gateway. It is the language of international commerce, scientific publication,the global internet, the professional services sector, and the IT industry that employs hundreds of thousands across South Asia. It is the language of every multinational corporation that has ever considered investing in the country, and of the diplomatic, legal, and financial systems with which any modern economy must engage. A Sri Lankan who speaks fluent English gains access to a job market extending from Colombo to Singapore to London. A Sri Lankan who does not is confined, with very few exceptions, to a domestic economy that cannot generate enough employment for its existing workforce.

The JVP, through its university apparatus, systematically stigmatised English as the language of the coloniser, the oppressor, and the class enemy. Speaking English on campus was treated as a political transgression, an act of class betrayal. Students who arrived with English proficiency were singled out during ragging, mocked, pressured to abandon the language, and taught to associate English fluency not with opportunity, but with complicity in an unjust system. The result was a generation of graduates who were not merely untrained in English, but actively hostile to it.

They did not lack English simply because the state failed to teach it, although the state did fail. They lacked English because a political movement that controlled their social environment for four formative years taught them that learning it was a moral failing. Meanwhile, every JVP leader who has ever engaged with the international community, including Tilvin Silva on his diplomatic missions to India and China, has relied on translators, English-speaking officials, and the very linguistic infrastructure the party spent decades undermining. The party that told a generation of students that English was the language of the oppressor now leads a government that cannot function internationally without it.

And the students who listened? The ones who internalised the message, refused to learn the language, and graduated monolingual into a bilingual job market? They are driving three-wheelers. They are stocking shelves. They are standing in queues at foreign employment agencies, waiting for contracts to work as manual labourers in the Middle East, because a degree from a Sri Lankan state university combined with fluency in Sinhala alone is not, and has never been, sufficient qualification for the professional employment they were promised. The man in the SUV, the one the JVP told them to blame, almost certainly speaks English. His children certainly do. The JVP ensured that the children of the poor would not.

Sri Lanka's youth unemployment rate has consistently ranked among the highest in South Asia, and the unemployment rate among arts and humanities graduates from state universities is staggering by any international benchmark. Surveys by the Department of Census and Statistics have repeatedly demonstrated that state university graduates take longer to find employment than their counterparts from technical colleges and vocational training institutes: institutions that JVP ideology considers inferior. A graduate of the University of Ruhuna with a degree in political science, shaped by a curriculum that has not been substantially revised in decades, delivered in a language that restricts them to the domestic labour market, and supplemented by four years of ideological instruction in the inherent injustice of capitalism, is less employable than a vocational institute graduate who learned to repair air conditioners. The air-conditioning technician earns a living. The political science graduate, burdened with a sophisticated vocabulary of grievance and no practical skills whatsoever, does not.

This is not an argument against the humanities. The humanities, when taught well, produce the critical thinkers, analysts,writers, and public intellectuals that any democracy requires. But the humanities taught under the JVP's ideological supervision do not produce critical thinkers; they produce cadres. They produce young men and women who can recite the contradictions of capitalism but cannot draft a business proposal, who can articulate the theory of surplus value but cannot prepare a tax return, who can explain dependency theory but cannot navigate a basic job interview, who understand in granular theoretical detail why the system is rigged against them, and who are, precisely because of this conditioning, incapable of functioning within the economy as it exists. The JVP did not arm these students with knowledge. It armed them with grievance. And grievance, however theoretically sophisticated, does not pay rent.

The irony is so bitter it would be comic were its consequences not measured in ruined lives. The JVP, having spent forty years teaching university students that wealth is theft, that the private sector is the enemy, that individual aspiration is collaboration, and that the only solution to poverty is political struggle rather than economic participation, won the presidency in 2024 on a platform that championed economic development, foreign investment, and engagement with the International Monetary Fund.

The same party that taught a generation of graduates to despise the market economy now governs a country that depends entirely on that market economy for its survival. The same party that told students the IMF was an instrument of imperialist subjugation now implements an IMF programme. The same party that stigmatised English now sends its General Secretary on English-dependent diplomatic missions. The same party that opposed private enterprise now courts foreign direct investment.

The pivot has been seamless. The party has altered its position because, as Tilvin Silva would say, the world has changed.But the graduates have not changed. They remain out there: tens of thousands of them, scattered across the country, armed with degrees that qualify them for virtually nothing, possessed of an ideology that explains everything while solving nothing, unable to speak the language of the modern economy, and trained to blame a class enemy for problems created in substantial part by the very political movement that claimed to be their champion. They were told the SUV was the problem. They were never told that the party pointing at the SUV was using their anger as fuel for its own ascent to power, and that once power was achieved, the party would quietly abandon every position it had urged them to fight for,leaving them standing in the wreckage of their own miseducation with nothing but a slogan and a degree that depreciates with each passing year.

The JVP's defenders will argue that the party gave voice to the voiceless, stood for rural students against the Colombo elite, fought for free education, resisted the commodification of knowledge, and defended the dignity of Sinhala-speaking,state-educated, working-class youth against an exclusionary system. This is true only in the sense that a man who locks you in a room and throws away the key has provided you with shelter.

The JVP did not defend free education; it captured it. It took an institution designed to liberate the children of the poor and converted it into a recruitment pipeline for a political party. It did not protect students from the elite; it ensured they could never compete with the elite, because competing requires the very skills the party spent four years ensuring they would never acquire. It did not give voice to the voiceless; it handed them a script (written by the party, approved by the party, and serving the party) and then told them that reciting it was the same as speaking for themselves.

The student from Hambantota who wanted to learn English was told that wanting to learn English made her a class traitor.The student from Matara who wanted to start a business was told that entrepreneurship was exploitation. The student from Badulla who sought an internship at a Colombo firm was told that the firm was the enemy. The student from Monaragala who simply wanted a job, any job that would allow him to repay his parents' sacrifices and build a decent life, was told that seeking employment in the private sector was ideological surrender. And then, when all these students graduated into unemployment, the JVP pointed at the man in the SUV and said: he did this to you.

He did not. The man in the SUV may well be corrupt. He may have evaded taxes, bribed officials, exploited workers, and accumulated wealth through means that would not survive scrutiny. Sri Lanka has no shortage of such figures, and the anger directed toward them is not entirely misplaced. But the man in the SUV did not design the state university curriculum. He did not enforce ragging. He did not call the strikes that added wasted semesters to degree programmes. He did not stigmatise the English language. He did not oppose the establishment of private universities. He did not teach a generation of students that learning marketable skills was an act of class betrayal. He did not build the ideological apparatus that took the brightest young minds in the country and systematically stripped them of every practical tool required to succeed.

The JVP did all of that. And then it won an election by promising to fix the very problems it spent forty years creating.

There is a word for taking a generation of young people (the most talented, hardworking, and deserving youth a country produces), feeding them an ideology that renders them permanently incapable of economic self-sufficiency, and then harvesting their resulting desperation as political leverage. The word is not liberation. The word is not education. The word is not social justice. The word is exploitation. And the JVP, a party that constructed its entire identity on opposing exploitation, has practiced it more systematically, more effectively, and over a longer duration than any corporate interest it has ever condemned. Forty years. Three hundred thousand students. A generation taught to blame a vehicle for the condition of a road built, deliberately, by the party that promised to carry them. That is the JVP's enduring contribution to higher education in Sri Lanka. And the man in the SUV had nothing to do with it.

text:
What to Expect from the Markets this Week – 2 November 2026

Nigeria’s financial markets closed the week ended 30 October 2026 with mixed results across asset classes. The @ngxgrp All-Share Index rose 2.86% to 254,299.49 points, ending a run of four losing weeks. The naira appreciated 1.16% to N1,346.26 per US dollar at the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market, and average Treasury bill and FGN bond yields moved by only a few basis points.

Banking system liquidity rose to N7.37trn from N6.94trn, and Standing Deposit Facility placements increased to N7.19trn from N6.78trn. The Open Repo Rate held at 20.00%, while the overnight rate rose 2bps to 20.38%. Average Treasury bill yields rose 1bp to 17.99%, and OMO bill yields rose to 18.59%. The 28 October NTB auction drew subscriptions of N1.91trn against an offer of N800bn, with N1.84trn of that demand placed on the 364-day bill. Stop rates fell on all three tenors, to 15.40%, 15.79% and 15.80%, and total allotment was N71.16bn. The parallel market rate weakened 0.72% to N1,385 per US dollar, which widened the FX premium to 2.88% from 0.97% a week earlier.

The Industrial Goods Index gained 14.58% over the week and @DangoteCement rose 27.81%, while the Banking Index fell 3.42% and FIRSTHOLDCO declined 17.31%. Thirty-three equities advanced and forty-eight declined. Turnover rose to 7.62bn shares worth N637.83bn in 192,138 deals, from 2.02bn shares worth N110.77bn in 173,113 deals the previous week. Financial services stocks accounted for 91.75% of the volume and 89.91% of the value traded. On the unlisted market, the @NASDNG Index fell 1.45% to 4,282.07 points. The Dangote Petroleum Refinery IPO, priced at N525 per share, has closed and allotment is pending. OPay listed on the New York Stock Exchange after raising US$304m at US$19 per share.

In a State of the Economy presentation to the Federal Executive Council on 28 October, the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, @taiwoyedele, reported GDP growth of 4.43% for Q2 2026, headline inflation of 14.63% and food inflation of 19.59% for September, and gross external reserves of US$55.1bn as at 9 October. He set a target of single-digit headline inflation by the end of 2027. President @officialABAT has asked the National Assembly to approve an external borrowing plan of US$20.52bn and €1.045bn for 2026 to 2027, and the Senate has referred the request to its Committee on Local and Foreign Debts. The CBN’s Q2 2026 economic report shows portfolio inflows up 17.6% quarter on quarter to US$7.09bn, while foreign direct investment rose 11.7% to US$1.15bn. In global commodities, Brent fell 2.86% to US$113.65 per barrel and WTI rose 0.91% to US$104.12 per barrel. Gold fell 2.61% to US$3,896.21 per ounce and silver fell 9.11% to US$49.18 per ounce.

The calendar for the week ahead opens with the @StanbicIBTC Nigeria PMI for October on 2 November. It then has October composite PMIs for the Eurozone, the United Kingdom and the United States on 4 November, the Bank of England’s rate decision on 5 November and Ghana’s October inflation figures on 6 November. On the domestic side, Proshare will track the allotment of the Dangote Petroleum Refinery IPO, Q3 earnings releases, the next NTB auction against the 28 October stop rates and allotment, and the gap between the official and parallel market naira rates.

text:
Dacoity. That is the word two Supreme Court judges used on 27 October for steep hospital markups.

The bench was hearing a petition seeking stricter price controls on medicines and medical consumables. A lawyer for private hospitals warned that forced margin cuts could make hospitals collapse. The bench said hospitals could survive by other means, "Not through this dacoity." The Court has reserved its order.

So how can a patient spot a markup on a bill? I built https://t.co/jCkw8RGzH5 and have added a consumables page. Pick an item, type the billed amount, and see what Rajasthan pays in bulk, before GST.

A 5 ml syringe with needle costs that state ₹1.29.

Private hospitals usually pay more than a state buying in bulk, so the gap is not proof of overcharging. The Court has not adopted this list.

Until the Court rules, the page offers one fixed point: what a state pays for the same item.

text:
Purpose of This tweet

1-The quiet crisis in our healthcare system starts with an artificial disparity: insurance packages sanctioned for corporate hospital chains are dramatically higher than those offered to standard 100-bed smaller hospital for the exact same procedures.

2-. If a surgeon earns ₹1,00,000 for an operation at a corporate hospital versus ₹30,000 in smaller hospitals, then why they will operate in smaller hospitals ( Many corporates allow visiting consultants)

3- It also fuels a troubling referral pipeline. Inflated corporate packages leave room for substantial kickbacks to referring physicians. Regrettably, patients are often steered toward whichever facility offers the referring doctor the highest financial cut.

4- Insurers fuel this loop because "cashless tie-ups with top corporate networks" are their primary marketing USP. To keep those prominent names on their roster, insurers routinely approve inflated corporate bills that they would aggressively slash for smaller clinics.

5-From the patient’s viewpoint, the choice seems obvious: why pay out of pocket or deal with reimbursement friction at a local clinic when corporate care is promoted as 100% cashless and fully covered?

6-The fallout is systemic. Independent nursing homes and smaller hospitals face shrinking volumes and non-viable margins. One by one, neighborhood healthcare institutions are being forced to shutter.

7-Once community clinics disappear, corporate monopolies take over. Without local competition, private networks can—and will—raise procedure rates unchecked, knowing patients have nowhere else to go.

8-Insurers will continue approving these escalating corporate costs because corporate branding drives policy sales, passing the total expense directly onto the policyholder.

9-The ultimate consequence for ordinary citizens: your annual health insurance premiums will surge year after year, and you will have no cheaper, viable alternatives left to turn to.

10-This consolidation is already well underway across Tier-1 metros. Unless policy pricing and network equity are regulated, the death of affordable community healthcare will soon sweep Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities as well.

text:
I recently learned about the staggering gap in surgical pricing across Mumbai:
​100-bed suburban hospital: ₹1.3 lakh
​Corporate hospital (e.g., Hinduja): ₹6.5 lakh for laparoscopic Hysterectomy ( Packages by Insurance company )
​Ayushman Bharat scheme: ~₹50,000
​Same surgery, identical clinical procedure—a 5x ro 10x price difference.
​Why are insurance companies willing to clear inflated corporate bills worth ₹6.5 lakh without hesitation, but aggressively scrutinize and delay a genuine ₹1 lakh claim from a smaller nursing home?
​The end victim is the regular consumer. Massive payouts to corporate hospitals drive up overall claim expenditure, which insurance companies directly pass on to you through surging annual premiums.
​If mid-sized hospitals are squeezed out, corporate monopolies will be the only option left. Corporate hospitals certainly deserve a premium for infrastructure, but unchecked billing requires regulatory limits.

text:
● #RelaxationDay

October 30 is Relaxation Day. You finish a day with your shoulders still tense, and only then do you notice. Surely everyone has had that experience.

The day was established by the #JapanRelaxationIndustryAssociation, a general incorporated association. It was founded to promote the relaxation industry, which offers rest and relief from tension for mind and body. Its date comes from October 30, 2013 (Heisei 25), the day the #StandardIndustrialClassificationOfJapan, issued by the #MinistryOfInternalAffairsAndCommunications, announced the newly created category "relaxation services (using manual techniques)."

The aim is the healthy growth of relaxation businesses and greater public awareness through safe, secure and stable services. The anniversary is certified and registered by the Japan Anniversary Association. The association runs a range of activities, including an insurance system specialized for relaxation services, the #RelaxationTherapistCertificationExam and the #RelaxationContest.

Relaxation means rest, recreation and loosening. It refers to a state in which the excitement of the #SympatheticNervousSystem is suppressed, the #ParasympatheticNervousSystem becomes dominant and tension is released. In the relaxation industry, the term generally refers to treatments that use manual techniques to ease tension in mind and body.

Modern life makes us surprisingly poor at resting. When schedules fill up, rest is easily put off. That relaxation services were placed within an industrial classification can be read as a sign that rest has come to be recognized as a valuable activity in society. For that reason, let us make today a day to practice resting on purpose.

Why not book some rest for yourself today? Visit a nearby treatment room, or soak slowly in a bath at home. Even stepping away from your smartphone for ten deep breaths is enough. Once your body has loosened, we close with a livelier topic: food.

text:
Everyone remembers the Mahabharata as a war. It actually started as a land dispute.

The Pandavas' last offer was five villages. Just five. Krishna took it to Duryodhana, who said no, not even as much land as a needle's point can pierce. Eighteen days later, you know the rest.

Now put the same fight in 2026. Nobody raises an army; it's cheaper that way. Duryodhana walks into a police station with one line from the argument, "they said we'd hear from them", and files a complaint of criminal intimidation.

Read that line again. Where's the threat? Injury to whose person, reputation, or property? Was it said to scare someone, or is it two families who both think the same land is theirs?

Who owns the land is a civil question, and it has a court of its own.

When something like this reaches the High Court, two questions do most of the work. What does the paper actually say? And what does the calendar say: who complained first, and what happened the day before the FIR? A lot of quash petitions are just those two questions in very formal English.

The Mahabharata needed a war to settle this. We at least have a procedure.

Which feud have you seen that should have been a civil suit and ended up at a police station?

text:
April 30, 1945. In a bunker under the Chancellery, Adolf Hitler has about one afternoon left to live.

A few hundred yards north, Soviet infantry are looking across the Königsplatz at the Reichstag. The building hadn't been used as a parliament since the 1933 fire, but to the Red Army it was the symbol of the whole Reich. It was the place they had been promised since Moscow, since Stalingrad, since Kursk. Stalin wanted it taken by May 1 so the news could reach Moscow for the May Day parade.

That deadline was going to cost a lot of lives.

Getting to the building meant crossing open ground cut by a flooded ditch, trenches, and bunkers, with 128mm flak guns firing in from a concrete tower 2 km away. Holding it were more than 1,000 Germans, a mix of Wehrmacht, Waffen-SS, old men from the Volkssturm, and teenage naval cadets shipped in from Rostock. Nobody in there was getting out alive unless they surrendered, and nobody was surrendering yet.

The first assault went in that morning and was shredded in the crossfire. So were two more before mid-afternoon.

At 1 p.m., 89 guns and rocket launchers fired at the building from close range. Soviet infantry even fired captured German Panzerfausts at it. Then the men ran.

Captain Stepan Neustroev's battalion reached the main entrance. They threw grenades through the doorway, went in after them, and took the ground floor fast.

Then they realized what they had walked into. The upper floors were full of Germans, and so was the maze of cellars beneath them, which held even more.

What followed was the kind of fighting nobody makes recruiting posters about. Stairwells were cleared with grenades, and machine guns covered every hallway. Men fought hand to hand in rooms so thick with smoke and plaster dust they couldn't see the man in front of them. Part of the building caught fire, and to this day nobody is sure whether the shelling started it or the Germans set it on purpose.

Col. Fyodor Zinchenko, whose 756th Rifle Regiment led the attack, wrote it plainly: "Inside the building, everything was burning and rumbling, the rooms were filled with smoke."

Sergeants Mikhail Yegorov and Meliton Kantaria were scouts carrying Red Banner No. 5, one of nine flags the 3rd Shock Army had issued to its divisions for exactly this moment. They fought up the stairs with grenades and hung it from a second-floor window. Every push toward the third floor got thrown back.

Kantaria, decades later: "Our banner fluttered wherever there was fighting."

Around 6 p.m. the Soviets finally blasted through the machine gun nests and took the third floor. That left roughly 300 of them holding the building above, with a larger, heavily armed German force underneath them in the basement. The Germans kept coming up out of the cellars to counterattack.

Around 10:40 that night, Sgt. Mikhail Minin and three men felt their way up a dark staircase to the roof. Only one of them had a flashlight. Minin admitted later that "we had no flag with us." They found a pole and a scrap of red cloth and jammed it into the statue on the roof.

The Soviets would later claim the Reichstag fell that night. It hadn't. The Germans still in the building went up the next day and tore Minin's flag down.

Around 3 a.m. on May 1, Yegorov and Kantaria went back up with Lt. Alexei Berest and planted Banner No. 5 on the roof. This is the flag Russia still calls the Victory Banner. Climbing the shattered glass dome cut their palms so badly that both carried the scars for the rest of their lives.

The fire wasn't put out until mid-afternoon on May 1. By evening the building was completely surrounded, and the Germans in the basement asked to talk.

Berest went down into that cellar posing as a colonel. The Germans tried to bargain over terms. They were told the only thing on offer was unconditional surrender.

Early on May 2, the survivors climbed out of the basement. Soviet figures put German dead in and around the Reichstag at more than 2,500. Soviet losses were never reliably counted.

What happened next is my favorite part. The men who took the building pulled out knives, chalk, and lumps of charcoal and covered the walls with their names, their hometowns, and what they thought of Germany. When the Reichstag was rebuilt in the 1990s, many of those scrawls were deliberately preserved. You can still see them inside the Bundestag today.

The men who were actually there didn't all get their due. Kantaria and Yegorov became Heroes of the Soviet Union. Berest was struck from the award list, later fell out with the Soviet government, and was sent to a labor camp.

And the photo everyone knows? It doesn't show any of them. Yevgeny Khaldei took it on May 2, after the fighting was over. He had flown in with three red tablecloths from the TASS office that his uncle, a tailor, sewed into flags overnight. He had soldiers pose on the roof and shot 36 frames.

When he developed them, he noticed the soldier steadying the flag-bearer was wearing two wristwatches. That was a dead giveaway for looting, so Khaldei scratched one off the negative with a needle.

So the most famous image of the end of the war in Europe is staged, retouched, and shows a flag made from tablecloths. The real flags went up in the dark, while men were still dying in the basement.

Fourth Army Area Commander and Director of Internal Security Operations Command (ISOC) Region 4 Lt. Gen. Chakrit Ucharatana has been officially appointed as Honorary Advisor to Pattani Football Club (Pattani FC).

​This appointment supports ongoing efforts to promote peace, strengthen community relations, and encourage public participation through sports in Thailand's southern border provinces.

Effective October 30, 2026, the appointment was formally authorized by Pattani FC President Assistant Professor Dr. Worawit Baru. As Honorary Advisor, Lt. Gen. Chakrit will offer management guidance to raise professional football standards, develop young athletes, and enhance cooperation between local communities and government agencies.

​This appointment follows discussions between Pattani FC executives and the Fourth Army Area Commander regarding potential cooperation to strengthen the club and its surrounding communities.

Pattani FC enjoys strong local support and serves as a key source of community pride and unity in the southern border provinces.

The Fourth Army Area and ISOC Region 4 Forward Command have expressed their readiness to support the club and participate in its activities, using football to stimulate the local economy, build community networks, and promote mutual understanding.

​This cooperation also aims to reduce misunderstandings between communities and authorities while supporting long-term peacebuilding efforts in the region.

Lt. Gen. Chakrit has also expressed his willingness to advise other sports teams across all 14 southern provinces, where appropriate and within his capacity. He emphasized that promoting sports creates opportunities for young people and helps lay the foundation for their future development.

text:
DR. YAWUTAMA EMMANUEL AMAZA (DR. YEA) - THE MAKING OF A GENERATIONAL LEADER 

In every generation, destiny raises certain individuals whose lives become a beacon of hope and a testament to the power of diligence, vision, and unwavering commitment to humanity. Such is the story of Dr Yawutama Emmanuel Amaza, a distinguished son of Borno State whose remarkable journey from a precocious young scholar to a formidable agent of change stands as an inspiration to the youth of Nigeria and beyond. Trained in the prestigious halls of Russian medical institutions and mentored under the visionary leadership of His Excellency Mr Peter Gregory Obi and His Excellency Eng. Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, Dr Amaza embodies the new breed of Nigerian leaders, competent, compassionate, and courageously committed to the transformation of his constituency. 

The Early Years: A Prodigy Emerges 

The year 2004 marked the beginning of an extraordinary academic journey when the young Yawutama Emmanuel Amaza underwent rigorous intellectual training far beyond his years, studying alongside seniors and earning the affectionate moniker "SM"—Small but Mighty. This early recognition foreshadowed the remarkable achievements that would follow.

In 2005, Mr Amaza's brilliance became undeniable as he emerged as the Best National Common Entrance Student in Borno State, the Best Student in Namu Schools, the Best Mathematician in Borno State, and the Best Mathematician in North Eastern Nigeria in a competition organised by the Nigerian Turkish International College (NTIC). His exceptional performance attracted scholarships from three prominent secondary schools: Nigerian Turkish International College, Namu Secondary School, and the prestigious School for the Gifted and Talented (Federal Government Academy, Suleja), where he secured a 100% scholarship, a testament to his exceptional intellectual capacity. 

From 2005 to 2011, while attending the School for the Gifted and Talented, Nigeria's premier institution for the nation's brightest students, Yawutama Emmanuel Amaza distinguished himself as the only Northerner to consistently rank among the top three students every term. His academic prowess continued to shine as he won a lottery during Nigeria's 50th Golden Jubilee celebration organised by Coca-Cola in 2010. 

In 2011, the young champion graduated with the Best WAEC Result in Borno State, achieving an unprecedented 9 Distinctions. That same year, he scored 274 in JAMB, arguably the best result from Borno State, a record yet to be surpassed by any candidate from the state. Demonstrating his early commitment to service, Dr Amaza worked as a volunteer teacher at Choice Private School, Maiduguri, gaining invaluable work experience at a remarkably young age.

The Road to Russia: A Destiny Fulfilled 

Dr Amaza's pursuit of higher education saw him secure admission to Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria (2011), University of Maiduguri (2012), and ultimately Rostov Medical University, Russia (2013). While at the University of Maiduguri, he benefited from the AGBAMI Chevron Scholarship and Total Petroleum Scholarship, further validating his academic excellence.
In 2013, Dr Yawutama Emmanuel Amaza emerged as a beneficiary of the Federal Scholarship Board under the Bilateral Education Agreement (BEA) to study MBBS abroad in Russia. In an era when communication networks were unreliable, divine providence led Dr Amaza to Abuja, where he received the life-transforming call that would reshape his destiny. The Federal Government scholarship covered $6,950 per year for seven years for upkeep, free tuition from the Russian Government, and free accommodation from the university, a comprehensive package that enabled him to focus entirely on his studies. 

From 2013 to 2014, Dr Amaza studied Russian Language at Rostov Medical University, Rostov-on-Don, after which he was granted the privilege of choosing any medical university of his choice. He proceeded to Stavropol Medical University, Stavropol, where he studied MBBS and graduated in 2020. Remarkably, for fifteen consecutive years (2005-2020), Dr Amaza was on fully funded scholarships, never paying school or tuition fees, a testament to his exceptional intellectual gifts and the grace that has followed his journey. 

Since 2016, Dr Amaza has successfully run his own business enterprise. Following his graduation in 2020, he has practised his medical profession while also serving as a Customs Broker in Russia since 2019. In 2021, he married and is blessed with two beautiful children, balancing family life with his numerous professional and community commitments.

A Voice for His People: Leadership and Advocacy 

Dr Amaza's leadership credentials extend far beyond his professional achievements. Since 2013, he has served as the Founder and President of Bura-Pabir Nation, Worldwide (BPN-WW), raising numerous Bura-Pabir content creators on social media and fostering unity among his people. In 2023, he sponsored the celebration of the 10th anniversary of the Bura-Pabir Nation group, which birthed a new movement and saw the adoption of Tarku (Garden Egg) as a widely accepted worldwide symbol of the Bura-Pabir People. 

His advocacy for his people has yielded tangible results. In 2024, Dr Amaza led the mass public outcry and mobilisation that successfully ended the merging of Nigerian Army University, Biu, with the Nigerian Defence Academy, Kaduna. In 2025, he again led the public outcry and mobilisation that prevented the conversion of Nigerian Army University, Biu, to Federal University, Biu.

Compassion in Action: Philanthropy and Community Service
Dr Amaza's philanthropic gestures speak volumes about his character. In 2025, he celebrated Children's Day by supplying the Federal Orthopaedic Hospital, Azare, Hawul, with hygiene materials for future use. That same year, he led the public fundraising, intervention, and outcry to help victims of the Hawul River Flooding, which left over 150 collapsed houses and over 500 farmlands that had been planted three times but washed away.

His intervention also helped mediate between Senator Mohammed Ali Ndume and Barr. Daniel Bwala through outreach to Channels Television and Arise TV, thereby ending their rivalry. He also led the public outcry to upgrade Annex Girasa Primary School to a full-fledged primary school under SUBEB, ensuring it was included in Borno State's budget allocation. 

In 2026, Dr Amaza celebrated Women's Day by supplying General Hospital, Marama, with hygiene and baby materials distributed to all expectant and postpartum women. He also led the public outcry to include Hawul LGA in INEC's proposal for delineation, dualization, and creation of new state constituencies in Borno State.

Championing Youth and Community Development 

Since 2025, Dr Amaza has served as the Convener for the Creation of Savannah State out of Borno State, proposing 24 new Local Government Areas for the proposed state and advocating for three new LGAs (Askira, Uba, and Lassa) out of Askira-Uba instead of only two. He also serves as Founder and President of the Conference of Southern Borno Youth Associations (COSB-YA), where he delivered the first physical Youth Conference in Borno South at Biu Stadium against all odds and hurdles.

The Call to Serve: A Mandate from the People 

In 2026, the people of Askira-Uba and Hawul Federal Constituency, recognising his exceptional qualities, called out with one voice: "Who shall we send? Who will go for us? Who will represent us?" The call for Dr Yawutama Emmanuel Amaza grew in momentum until he hearkened unto the voice of his people and declared his intention to serve as House of Representatives Member for Askira-Uba and Hawul Federal Constituency. 

The people of Askira-Uba adopted and accepted Dr Amaza as their own bona fide son, bestowing upon him the native name Dr Mamza. Now known as Dr Mamza, he has led a rigorous, revolutionary, and pace-setting political campaign never seen before in recent memory, going from house to house, unit to unit, ward to ward, from Hawul LGA to Askira-Uba LGA, in his bid to answer the call of his people. 

In September 2026, Dr Amaza emerged as the NDC candidate for House of Representatives, Askira-Uba/Hawul Federal Constituency, with INEC officially approving his candidature. As the only youth on the ballot for House of Representatives and the only INEC-approved candidate from Hawul LGA, Dr Amaza represents the ticket of the youth, a testament to the NDC party's commitment to youth representation and inclusion.

The Mentorship Connection 

Dr Amaza's political philosophy and leadership approach have been profoundly shaped by the mentorship and tutelage of two of Nigeria's most visionary leaders: His Excellency Mr Peter Gregory Obi and His Excellency Eng. Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso. From Mr Obi, he has imbibed the principles of prudent resource management, transformative leadership, and unwavering commitment to the common good. From Eng. Kwankwaso, he has learned the importance of grassroots mobilisation, educational empowerment, and infrastructure development that touches the lives of ordinary citizens. 

These mentors have instilled in Dr Amaza the conviction that leadership is not about personal aggrandisement but about service, sacrifice, and the transformation of lives. They have taught him that the youth are not too young to run, win, and lead, a philosophy he now embodies as he steps forward to represent his people. 

Dr Amaza's vision for his constituency is one of comprehensive transformation, from infrastructure development to educational advancement, from healthcare delivery to agricultural modernisation, from youth empowerment to women's inclusion. His campaign is anchored on the belief that truth and Amana (trust) lie with the youth, whose progressive ideas, vision, fearlessness, and strength represent the glory of their generation.

A Call to Support a Worthy Leader

The story of Dr Yawutama Emmanuel Amaza is a compelling narrative of what is possible when talent, focus, hard work, divine favour, and genuine love for humanity converge. From his days as a "Small but Mighty" academic prodigy to his emergence as a compassionate physician, successful entrepreneur, and passionate community advocate, Dr Amaza has consistently demonstrated that he possesses the character, competence, and commitment to deliver transformative leadership. 

As the people of Askira-Uba and Hawul Federal Constituency prepare to make a historic decision, Dr Amaza offers himself as a servant-leader, one who has never forgotten his roots, one who has consistently used his resources and influence to uplift his people, and one who represents the future of Nigeria's youth. He is not just a candidate; he is a movement, a symbol of hope, and a testament to the boundless possibilities that await when we give youth a chance. 

Let us embrace this worthy son of the soil. Let us love him, share his story, and support his candidacy. Let us send a clear message that in Askira-Uba and Hawul Federal Constituency, competence matters, character matters, and the future belongs to those who dare to dream and work for it. 

Dr Yawutama Emmanuel Amaza, Dr Wakanda, the only youth on the ballot, the ticket of the youth, is ready to serve. The time to support him is now. Together, we can build a better tomorrow, a brighter future, and a new era of prosperity for all.

text:
Marshal Mikhail Nikolayevich Tukhachevsky (1893-1937), nicknamed the "Red Napoleon," was a brilliant Soviet military commander, theorist, and one of the youngest Marshals of the Soviet Union. His life story spans a rapid rise through the ranks of war, pioneering military innovations, and a tragic fall during Joseph Stalin’s Great Purge....

After the October Revolution, Tukhachevsky joined the Bolsheviks and the newly formed Red Army in 1918, gaining the backing of Leon Trotsky. He quickly proved his ruthless effectiveness, leading the defense of Moscow, fighting on the Eastern Front against Admiral Alexander Kolchak, and commanding forces in the Caucasus and the Polish–Soviet War (including the 1920 attack on Warsaw). He led the suppression of major anti-Bolshevik peasant revolts, such as the Tambov Uprising, where historical debates and records note the harsh measures and use of chemical irritants against insurgents.

As a visionary theoretician, he pioneered the "theory of deep operations," advocating for mechanized corps, mass tank formations, aviation, and airborne troops to break through enemy lines. His forward-thinking ideas laid the tactical foundation for Soviet victory on the Eastern Front in World War II, though many reforms were temporarily derailed by his death.

Tukhachevsky clashed with Joseph Stalin and Marshal Kliment Voroshilov, famously holding a grudge against Stalin over the strategic failure at the Battle of Warsaw in 1920. In May 1937, amidst Stalin’s paranoia and the onset of the Great Purge, Tukhachevsky was stripped of his post, arrested, and interrogated under brutal torture overseen by NKVD chief Nikolai Yezhov.

. . . .

On June 11, 1937, Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky stood before a secret Soviet military tribunal. He and seven other senior officers were accused of conspiracy and treason.

By the following morning, they had been executed.

One of the Red Army’s most prominent commanders had gone from marshal to condemned prisoner inside a prosecution later repudiated by the Soviet state itself.

Tukhachevsky was 44.

He had risen through the Civil War and become an influential military commander and theorist. His authority belonged to the Bolshevik system, not to an opposition movement challenging it.

He had helped build the army Stalin was now purging.

The accusations alleged an anti-Soviet military organization and collaboration with foreign enemies, including Nazi Germany.

Their existence in a prosecution file did not make them true.

The proceedings belonged to the Great Terror, when interrogations and confessions were used to manufacture the appearance of organized plots.

Accounts of the case describe coercion and torture. The defendants’ admissions cannot be read as freely given confirmation of the charges.

Nor should the familiar story of German intelligence feeding Stalin forged material be allowed to make the Soviet leadership disappear from its own prosecution.

The significance of alleged foreign forgeries remains debated. Stalin’s state arrested the officers, conducted the secret trial, and executed them.

Responsibility for those decisions was Soviet.

The trial offered no public opportunity to test the evidence. Its secrecy deprived the accused of the visibility that might have exposed contradictions to a wider audience.

The executions followed during the night of June 11–12.

The case accelerated the destruction of senior military leadership. Officers could become suspects because of professional connections to men who had already been arrested.

An army organized around chains of command was being taught that association itself could be fatal.
