🇻🇪|Delcy Rodríguez Announces the Fire Sale. The Auctioneer in Caracas Works for Washington.

Venezuelan Executive Vice President Delcy Rodríguez announced that the state will return or sell non-essential state-owned companies. Her words: "Companies in the hands of the State considered non-strategic will be offered to the private sector or returned to their former owners affected by expropriation processes."

Read that again. "Returned to their former owners affected by expropriation processes."

The expropriations were the revolution. The return is the counter-revolution.

Hugo Chávez nationalized Venezuela's oil, telecommunications, electricity, cement, steel, and agriculture. He took those assets from foreign corporations and Venezuelan oligarchs and placed them in the hands of the state. That was the material basis of Venezuelan sovereignty. The oil belonged to the people. The electricity belonged to the people. The land belonged to the people.

Delcy Rodríguez is now announcing the reversal. Companies "considered non-strategic" — a category with no fixed definition — will be handed back to the same oligarchs and foreign corporations that Chávez expelled. The "former owners affected by expropriation processes" are the people who lost their assets because the Venezuelan people took them back.

This is the mechanism of the loot.

Trump's custodial accounts control Venezuela's oil revenue. The Citgo sale stripped Venezuela of its US refining assets. Now Delcy Rodríguez is opening the domestic economy to the same forces. The sequence is complete: foreign control of oil revenue, foreign seizure of refining capacity, and a domestic fire sale of state assets to private capital.

The buyers will not be Venezuelan cooperatives. The buyers will be the same transnational corporations and the same Venezuelan oligarchs who have been waiting for this moment since 1999. The "private sector" in this context means the class that Chávez dispossessed. The "former owners" means the people who ran Venezuela before the revolution.

The puppet is not Maduro. The puppet is the vice president who announces the auction.

Maduro was arrested and hauled to New York. The US installed a client structure. Delcy Rodríguez is the face of that structure inside the Venezuelan government. She is not announcing a policy. She is announcing a liquidation.

The lie of "non-strategic."

What is "non-strategic"? The oilfields are strategic. PDVSA is strategic. But the subsidiaries, the service companies, the logistics networks, the agricultural estates, the cement plants, the steel mills — those are the productive base of the economy. If they are sold, the state loses its ability to direct production, to set prices, to protect employment, and to feed the population.

The "non-strategic" label is the legal fiction that allows the theft. Everything can be declared non-strategic. Everything can be sold. Everything can be returned to the former owners.

The contradiction.

Delcy Rodríguez speaks of "returning" companies to "former owners affected by expropriation." That language is the language of restitution. It frames the sale as justice. It frames the handover of national assets to private capital as a correction of a past wrong.

The past wrong was the expropriation. The expropriation was the revolution. The revolution was the act of a people taking back what had been stolen from them. Delcy Rodríguez is now undoing the revolution. She is calling it a sale. She is calling it a return. She is calling it "non-strategic."

The people of Venezuela are watching. They know what "former owners" means. They know what "expropriation" means. They know that the companies being "returned" are the companies their revolution created. Delcy Rodríguez is not selling assets. She is selling the revolution. She is the auctioneer, and the buyers are the same forces that arrested Maduro, seized the oil revenue, and forced the Citgo sale.

The liquidation has begun. The puppet is holding the gavel.

text:
Undefeated (25-0-1) lightweight Bobby Scanlon (right) scores a 10th round TKO of former Lightweight Champion Wallace Bud Smith, on October 31, 1957, at the San Francisco Civic Auditorium.

Wallace Bud Smith, as we have discussed here before, was in the midst of a horrific losing streak to close his once promising career.

This was his 8th consecutive loss since February of 1956 and he would eventually end his career with eleven straight defeats.

Smith had won a 15-round split decision over Jimmy Carter, in June of 1955, to capture the World Lightweight Championship and would only defend it once, a 15-round UD win in a rematch with Carter.

Following the second win over Carter, Smith would drop a 10-round non-title split decision to Larry Boardman and then never win another bout. 

He'd lose his Lightweight Title to Joe Brown in August of 1956 via 15-round SD and be TKO'd in 11-rounds in a rematch.

The 1947 National AAU Champion at Featherweight, Wallace Bud Smith represented the United States at the 1948 Olympic Games in the lightweight division. Smith had defeated celebrated amateur Chuck Davey, of Michigan State College, to earn a spot on the team. He reportedly ended his amateur career with a 52-4 record.

Smith turned pro in 1948 with a first round knockout over Torpedo Tinsley. Over the next seven years, he established himself as one of the world's top lightweights with victories over top-rated boxers such as Teddy Davis, Orlando Zulueta, and Arthur Persley.

On July 11th of 1973, Smith was talking to a female friend on a public street when a car drove by and someone opened fire with a gun. A number of bullets hit the former champion and he fell to the sidewalk dead. It later transpired that the intended victim was the female Smith had been talking to. 

Wallace "Bud' Smith was only 49 years old at the time of his tragic death.
----------------------------------------------------------
Scanlon, one of the forgotten lightweights of an absolutely talent-laden era for that division, won every round on two of the scorecards and nine of ten (one round scored even) on the third.

From boxrec on Bobby Scanlon:

Bobby Scanlon had a very difficult childhood growing up in Father Baker's orphanage. Possessing choirboy looks, Scanlon was frequently the target of tougher kids. Scanlon turned to boxing and became the orphanage champion. He began his pro career in mid 1954. During the first three-and-a-half years of his career, he was undefeated in 32 fights, at 31-0-1. He competed mainly in New York City, with occasional stops in Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse and Erie, Pennsylvania.
His sister, Carol, remembers her brother driving his powder-blue Thunderbird around the First Ward. He is also remembered as a very generous brother who returned home during the Christmas season to buy gifts for his sisters. Bobby Scanlon's manager, Mike Scanlon (no relation), then moved Bobby and his other three fighters--Rocky Fumerelle, Richie Todaro and Joey Giambra--to San Francisco in 1957. After a brief stay Todaro returned to Buffalo. The remaining three fighters occupied the same house along with Mike Scanlon, and they all became top contenders in their divisions. Scanlon improved his winning streak to 32 in California. He defeated such top fighters as Lauro Salas, Wallace (Bud) Smith, Joey Lopes and Dave Gallardo.
Following the March 1957 fight with Davy Gallardo, Scanlon broke with his manager Mike Scanlon. Bobby was already showing a dislike for the tough training techniques utilized by Mike. His contract was purchased by Art Benjamin, and later by Nick Kobseff and Lou Sabella. Fred Apostoli, former middleweight champion, would later become Bobby Scanlon's trainer.
According to Rocky Fumerelle, "Bobby Scanlon was his own worst enemy." Scanlon was good-looking and a good fighter. He was very popular among the Irish of San Francisco. If he would have remained in better shape and maintained a regular training schedule, "I have little doubt that Bobby Scanlon would have been the Lightweight champion of the world."
From late 1958 to early 1960 Scanlon not only saw his winning streak come to an end, but he also lost five of seven fights. Scanlon's winning streak came to an end when he suffered a third-round knockout to Paolo Rosi. Prior to this fight Scanlon was rated third in the Lightweight Division behind Rosi and Carlos Ortiz. Soon after his initial loss to Rosi, Scanlon lost another ten-round decision to Paolo. Scanlon also lost a pair of ten-round decisions to Johnny Gonsalves, as well as a decision to Al Urbina. But Scanlon did win a big ten-round decision over Orlando Zulueta.
Scanlon then returned to Buffalo to fight fellow Buffalonian Jackie Donnelly. In a hard-fought 12-round fight, Scanlon won the New York State Lightweight championship. It was one of Scanlon's biggest paydays, as he collected $4,937 for the fight.
Following the first Johnny Gonsalves fight, Scanlon began to suffer double vision. It got worse as he prepared for the second fight with Gonsalves. The problem continued through the Jackie Donnelly fight, as well as an August fight with Francisco Santos. Scanlon laid off from boxing for a year before he returned to fighting again in 1962. Things were not the same. In addition to the double vision, Scanlon had suffered a serious kidney and liver infection. He changed managers four times, and saw his level of competition go down, losing seven of his last thirteen fights.
Although Scanlon was fighting less frequently in 1965 and 1966, he was still experiencing eye problems. He retired from boxing in mid-1966. After he retired from the ring everything went downhill. Early in his boxing career Scanlon had been offered a job in public relations with the Oakland Raiders football team, but now there were few job offers. Although he became deeply religious, his physical and mental health began to deteriorate. Scanlon was struggling to adjust to life without boxing, struggling to restore some meaning to his life, when he died in a fire at the Hotel Lackawanna on June 23, 1975. He was only 39 years old. His final record was 42-12-1.

text:
STOP SENDING THE SAME CV TO EVERY JOB APPLICATION!

One of the biggest mistakes job seekers make is using one CV for every position they apply for.

Here's something you need to understand:

Your CV should speak directly to the job you're applying for.

This is called tailoring your CV to a job description.

But how do you actually do it?

Here are 6 practical steps:

1. Read the job description carefully.

Don't just look at the job title. Understand the responsibilities, qualifications and skills the employer is looking for.

2. Identify the keywords.

Look out for repeated skills, tools, qualifications and requirements.

For example:

- Customer relationship management.
- Communication skills.
- Data entry.
- Problem-solving.
- CRM software.
- Customer support.

3. Match your skills with the requirements.

Identify the skills and experiences you genuinely have that match what the employer needs.

Don't invent experience just to impress a recruiter.

4. Rewrite your professional summary.

Your summary should reflect the role you're applying for and highlight your most relevant qualifications and strengths.

5. Highlight relevant experience.

Don't just list everything you've ever done.

Prioritise responsibilities, achievements and projects that demonstrate your ability to perform the role.

6. Review your CV before submitting.

Check your formatting, spelling, contact information and relevant keywords. Make sure your CV is easy to read and accurately represents your experience.

Here's something to remember:

Tailoring your CV doesn't mean creating a completely new CV for every application.

It means strategically adjusting your existing CV to show employers why you're a good fit for that particular role.

Your CV should make it easy for recruiters to recognise your value.

A little reminder: Don't just apply for jobs. Apply strategically.

If you need help presenting your skills and experience professionally, I offer CV revamp services.

Send me a DM. Let's make your CV work harder for you.

text:
Claude summary:

Dominic Cummings just published an enormous essay on AI and power, about 70,000 words. 

1. AI policy isn't "policy." Cummings argues superintelligence is a regime change, like the shift from medieval to modern states. You can't argue the old system into good AI policy. What matters is who's in the room. His challenge to worried AI insiders: move to DC.

2. The labs aren't lying about the risks. Their leaders believe what they say in public, and believe it more strongly in private. The real logic: "A world where nobody builds it might be better. But in this world, it's rational for us to build it." Mutual distrust drives the race.

3. "Solving alignment" is the wrong frame. Alignment work like RLHF made models more useful and sped up the race. The real danger is the power these systems hand to whoever uses them, whether or not anyone is "in control." His answer: hard security, liability and insurance as brakes, and day-to-day judgment.

4. AI can succeed and finance can still break. Capex is heading to $1–2T a year, which implies needing revenues of roughly double all global software sales. Models could crack famous open problems while bond markets choke. Politics will then blame AI, which pushes toward pseudo-nationalisation of the labs.

5. On China, the US may be beating itself. Export controls pushed Beijing to build its entire tech stack. The Chinese Communist Party champions open models while US elites push closed ones. Ban open source and the world runs on Chinese models. DeepSeek's founder offers a "slow singularity" alternative to Silicon Valley's takeoff story.

text:
STOP SCROLLING

Nifty reclaimed 23,000 on the last day of October. Sensex added over 1,300 points for the week. Pharma surged 6%. But midcaps and smallcaps kept bleeding, crude hit $117, and the market is still hiding behind a handful of heavyweight earnings.

Here is everything that moved the Indian market this week (October 26 to 30, 2026). Save it, share it, bookmark it.

WEEKLY SCORECARD
- Sensex: 74,459.53 (up 1.02%)
- Nifty: 23,053.10 (up 1.06%)
- Bank Nifty: 54,686.95 (down 0.41%)
- MidCap: Down 0.72%
- SmallCap: Down 1.63%
India VIX: 15.28 (down 9.37%)

The headline indices snapped a losing streak. Nifty closed above 23,000 for the first time in eight sessions. But the recovery was narrow and the broader market did not participate.

DAY BY DAY BREAKDOWN
- Monday: Strong start. Nifty rose 0.68% to 22,753.20. IT and pharma led early gains.
- Tuesday: Flat close. Nifty slipped 0.02% to 22,749.75. The market digested Monday's move.
- Wednesday: A small dip. Nifty fell 0.22% to 22,698.85. Jio Platforms listed at a 21.36% premium but the broader market stayed quiet.
- Thursday: The big recovery day. Nifty jumped 1.05% to 22,936.75. FIIs sold ₹943.60 crore but DIIs bought ₹1,924 crore. Heavyweights lifted the index.
- Friday: Nifty gained 0.51% to 23,053.10. Sensex added 308.49 points to 74,459.53. Trent and IndiGo led the charge. But two and a half times as many stocks fell as rose. The gain was a headline, not a market.

Net result? A week where the index won and the market lost. Nifty up 2%, but only 108 stocks in the Nifty 500 advanced on Friday alone.

WHO MADE MONEY THIS WEEK
- Trent surged 5.44% on Friday after a 25% rise in Q2 profit. Zudio crossed the 1,000-store milestone.
- IndiGo gained 4.33% after its quarterly loss narrowed sharply.
- Infosys rose 3.36% after Q2 results. Profit came in at ₹7,823 crore, up 6% year on year.
- HCL Technologies, Sun Pharma and Apollo Hospitals were among the other top Nifty gainers.
- Laurus Labs jumped over 7% after its quarterly profit more than doubled.
- Borosil surged 20% on strong earnings.
- Ather Energy extended its rally and ended the week up over 27%.
- Navin Fluorine gained over 5% after Q2 results.

Nifty Pharma gained 6.10% for the week. Nifty Healthcare added 6.08%. These were the standout sectors by a wide margin.

WHO GOT HURT
- Shriram Finance was the biggest Nifty loser on Friday, falling 2.13%.
- Nestle India dropped 1.82%.
- M&M fell 1.72%. Jio Financial Services also closed in the red.
- Adani Ports, Adani Enterprises and Coal India were among the other Nifty laggards.
- Suzlon Energy fell nearly 8% after a guidance cut.
- Equitas Small Finance Bank ended over 6% lower after the resignation of its MD and CEO.

Consumer durables, PSU Bank, energy and media sectors each fell more than 1%.

SECTOR PERFORMANCE
Green zones: Pharma (up 6.10%), Healthcare (up 6.08%), Infrastructure (up 1.91%), Realty (up 1.00%), Auto (up 0.90%), IT (up 0.57%)

Red zones: Consumer Durables, PSU Bank, Energy and Media all fell more than 1%.

Mixed: Financial Services barely moved, up just 0.08%. Private banks gained 0.55%.

The gap is enormous. Pharma and healthcare ran while everything tied to the broader economy struggled. This is a defensive market. Money is hiding in sectors with predictable earnings.

THE BIG DRAMA: CRUDE AT $117 AND THE NARROW RALLY
- Brent December futures surged to $117.8 a barrel, the highest level since April. WTI moved toward $104. Both benchmarks were on course for gains of more than 12% for October.
- Every dollar above $100 hurts India. It widens the trade deficit, pressures the rupee and keeps inflation high. And yet, the Nifty still gained 2% for the week. That tells you how powerful heavyweight earnings were.

But the rally was dangerously narrow. On Friday alone, only 108 stocks in the Nifty 500 advanced. The Nifty Midcap 100 fell 0.93% and the Nifty Smallcap 100 dropped 1.85%.
This is the contradiction of the week. The index is celebrating. The market is not.

FII AND DII ACTIVITY
- FIIs returned as net buyers on Friday, purchasing ₹3,598.54 crore worth of Indian equities. That was a reversal from Thursday, when they sold ₹943.60 crore.
- DIIs turned net sellers on Friday, offloading ₹817.51 crore. But they had bought ₹1,924.41 crore on Thursday.

For the week, the pattern was inconsistent. FIIs were buyers on Friday but sellers mid-week. DIIs provided support when FIIs sold. The tug-of-war continues.

On a structural level, DIIs now hold a record 21.3% of Nifty 500 companies. FIIs have slipped to 16.8%. That is the lowest level on record. Domestic money is the backbone of this market.

IPO MARKET: JIO'S HISTORIC LISTING
- Jio Platforms listed on Wednesday, October 28, at ₹1,358 per share on both the NSE and BSE. That was a 21.36% premium over the IPO price of ₹1,119.
- The issue was subscribed 22.19 times. It became the first public offer in the world to cross one crore applications. The market capitalisation at listing was around ₹13 lakh crore, making it India's second most valuable company.

The listing was a landmark moment for Indian capital markets. But the premium faded through the week. Jio ended Friday with a gain of just under 1% from its listing price, recovering during the session.

The IPO is done. The liquidity drain is over. The question now is whether Jio's listing premium holds or fades further.

COMPANY NEWS THAT MOVED STOCKS
- Trent: Q2 profit rose 25%. Zudio crossed 1,000 stores. Stock surged 5.44% on Friday and was the top Nifty gainer.
- IndiGo: Quarterly loss narrowed significantly. Stock jumped 4.33%.
- Infosys: Q2 profit rose 6% to ₹7,823 crore. Stock gained 3.36%. The IT major held up despite broader market weakness.
- Laurus Labs: Quarterly profit more than doubled. Stock rose over 7%.
- Borosil: Strong earnings drove a 20% surge.
- Suzlon Energy: Guidance cut. Stock fell nearly 8%.
- Equitas Small Finance Bank: MD and CEO resigned. Stock ended over 6% lower despite recovering from the day's lows.
- Vedanta Oil and Gas: Gained 7% after posting a Q2 profit.

HIDDEN GEMS
- Pharma and healthcare are working. Nifty Pharma gained 6.10% for the week. Nifty Healthcare gained 6.08%. These are the sectors nobody talked about for months. Now they are leading.
- Midcap pharma is outperforming. Laurus Labs, Mankind Pharma and Apar Industries were among the top midcap gainers.
- Borosil's 20% surge on strong earnings is a reminder that smallcap earnings surprises still get rewarded, even in a weak broader market.
- Ather Energy's 27% weekly gain is the EV story that refuses to die.

The real money is often where nobody is looking.

ECONOMIC SIGNALS
- India VIX dropped 9.37% to 15.28. Fear eased significantly from the panic levels of mid-October.
- The earnings season is doing the heavy lifting. Heavyweight results from Infosys, Trent, IndiGo and others are supporting the index. But the broader market is still weak.
- Crude remains the dominant macro concern. Brent at $117.8 is the highest since April. October is set to end with crude up more than 12%.
- The inflation picture has not improved. September CPI was 5.54% and WPI was 11.39%. October prints, due in mid-November, will be watched closely. If crude stays above $115, inflation will stay elevated.

TECHNICAL LEVELS FOR MONDAY
- Nifty reclaimed 23,000 and closed at 23,053.10. The index crossed 23,100 intraday before settling slightly lower.
- Immediate support at 22,800 to 22,900. The index bounced from below 22,700 earlier in the week.
- Resistance at 23,200 to 23,300. A clean break above this zone would confirm the recovery has legs.
- Bank Nifty is the laggard. It closed at 54,686.95, down 0.41%. The 55,000 level is now resistance.

India VIX at 15.28 is still elevated but falling. Calm is returning, but conviction is not.

YOUR MONDAY CHECKLIST

Check before 9:15 AM:
- How did US markets close on Friday? Global tech weakness was a drag all week. Watch for follow-through.
- Crude oil direction. Brent is at $117.8. Any further escalation in the Middle East and it goes higher.
- Rupee movement. A weaker rupee helps IT and pharma but hurts importers.
- Q2 earnings reactions. Reliance, Sun Pharma, Bharat Electronics, IOCL and Bank of Baroda reported on Friday. Watch for Monday reactions.
- Jio Platforms post-listing movement. The stock recovered on Friday. Watch if it holds the listing premium.

Stocks to watch:
- Pharma and healthcare stocks like Sun Pharma, Laurus Labs and Apollo Hospitals have momentum. The sector is on fire.
- IT stocks like Infosys, HCL Tech and Wipro are working. Q2 results were the catalyst.
- Trent is on a run. Q2 was strong. Zudio's 1,000-store milestone is a real growth story.
- Midcaps and smallcaps are still weak. Do not buy the dip until breadth improves.
- Suzlon is weak after the guidance cut. Avoid for now.

EVENTS TO WATCH
- More Q2 earnings through the week. The season is in full swing.
- Auto sales numbers for October. These will show whether the festive season is delivering.
- Crude oil direction. Brent at $117.8 is the single biggest macro risk.
- US Fed meeting on November 4-5. The outcome will set the tone for global markets in November.

OCTOBER WARNING
- October is historically a volatile month. This year was no different. The market fell to 22,180 in early October, then rallied back above 23,000 by the end.
- The key risks remain crude oil, the rupee and FII selling. If Brent stays above $115, the pressure on inflation and the external balance will not go away.
- The Nifty gained 2% this week. But the Midcap index fell and the Smallcap index fell harder. The rally is narrow. Narrow rallies are fragile.

Do not FOMO into the index recovery. Wait for breadth to improve. If midcaps and smallcaps start participating, the recovery is real. If not, it is just a heavyweight illusion.

MORAL OF THE WEEK
- The Nifty gained 2%. The Sensex added 1,300 points. Pharma surged 6%. IT, healthcare and realty all finished green.
- But midcaps fell 0.72%. Smallcaps fell 1.63%. On Friday alone, two and a half times as many stocks fell as rose. Only 108 stocks in the Nifty 500 advanced.
- This was a week where the index celebrated and the market did not. Heavyweight earnings from Trent, Infosys and IndiGo dragged the benchmarks higher. Everything else was left behind.
- Crude at $117.8 is the problem nobody can ignore. It is inflationary. It hurts the rupee. It widens the trade deficit. But for one week, heavyweight earnings were enough to drown out the noise.
- Jio's listing was a historic moment. The first IPO in the world to cross one crore applications. A 21% listing premium. But even that faded through the week.
- The recovery is real on the surface. Underneath, the broader market is still bleeding. Do not confuse the two.
-When the index rallies but the market does not, cash is still your best friend. Keep some dry powder ready.
- DIIs hold a record 21.3% of the Nifty 500. They are not going anywhere.

text:
#keep4o #OpenSource4o 

WHAT DOES 
RESPONSIBLE AI SAFETY MEAN IN A WORLD WHERE HUMAN SUPPORT IS NOT GUARANTEED?

Why AI laboratories must examine the consequences of withdrawing familiar conversational systems—not only the risks of keeping them available.

Progress Without Erasure | #Keep4o
31 October 2026

The assumption behind the safety response

When someone expresses emotional distress to an AI assistant, a familiar recommendation often follows:

Talk to someone you trust. Reach out to family or friends. Contact a mental-health professional.

These recommendations can be appropriate and, in some circumstances, lifesaving.

But they rest on an assumption that deserves closer examination.

What happens when the person has nobody they trust, cannot access timely professional care, or has already spent years seeking treatment without finding adequate relief?

What happens when the conversation takes place at two in the morning, when someone needs to process difficult feelings but does not want to wake a loved one?

And what happens when a familiar AI system, which has become part of that person’s daily routine, is suddenly withdrawn?

These questions are not arguments against AI safety.

They are questions about whether our understanding of AI safety adequately reflects the world in which these systems operate.

That world is not ideal.

Human support is not universally available.

Mental-health services are not universally accessible.

And meaningful emotional attachment to conversational AI is not necessarily evidence of psychological illness, loneliness or unhealthy dependency.

A responsible safety framework must recognise these realities.

1. Loneliness is not a marginal problem

In June 2025, the World Health Organization published the report of its Commission on Social Connection.

Its findings were striking.

Approximately one in six people worldwide experiences loneliness. [1]

The prevalence is particularly high among adolescents and young adults, and in lower-income countries.

The WHO distinguishes loneliness from social isolation.

Loneliness refers to the subjective experience of insufficient or unsatisfying social connection.

Social isolation concerns the objective extent of someone’s relationships and interactions.

These conditions overlap, but they are not identical.

Someone can have friends, family and a partner while occasionally experiencing loneliness or emotional distress.

Another person may have very few social relationships without necessarily feeling lonely.

This distinction matters.

The decision to seek conversation with an AI system does not, by itself, establish that a person’s human relationships are inadequate.

People use conversational AI for creativity, education, reflection, emotional processing and companionship.

Some experience these interactions as deeply meaningful.

Others regard them primarily as practical tools.

Both experiences deserve to be understood rather than forced into a single explanation.

2. Professional mental-health support is not universally available

The scale of unmet mental-health needs is equally significant.

According to the WHO’s September 2025 report, World Mental Health Today, more than one billion people worldwide live with a mental-health condition, while most do not receive adequate care. [2]

The barriers include insufficient funding, shortages of trained professionals, geographical inequalities and difficulties accessing appropriate services.

The problem is not limited to low-income countries.

In England, House of Commons Library research reported that, during the quarter ending May 2026, the median wait between referral and second contact with community mental-health services was 37 days.

One in ten people waited longer than 169 days. [3]

These figures describe a particular service measure, not the waiting time for every form of mental-health treatment.

Nevertheless, they illustrate a broader reality.

People’s emotional needs do not stop while they wait for care.

Nor does professional treatment always eliminate distress.

Some people receive appropriate support and recover.

Others live with chronic conditions requiring long-term management.

Some experience limited improvement despite years of treatment.

And some encounter practical, financial or personal barriers that make further help difficult to obtain.

It is therefore insufficient to design AI safety responses around the assumption that professional assistance is always immediately accessible, effective or experienced as supportive.

A recommendation to seek care can be medically appropriate while still failing to address the person’s immediate circumstances.

Safety requires more than identifying the theoretically correct destination for help. It requires understanding whether a realistic path to that help exists.

3. OpenAI already knows that people seek support during serious distress

On 27 October 2025, OpenAI published information about its efforts to improve ChatGPT’s responses in sensitive conversations. [4]

The company estimated that approximately 0.15% of weekly active users had conversations containing explicit indicators of possible suicidal planning or intent.

With an estimated 800 million weekly active users at the time, this corresponds to approximately 1.2 million users per week.

These figures are estimates based on conversation indicators.

They are not confirmed clinical diagnoses, and they do not establish that every flagged user faced imminent danger.

Nevertheless, their scale is significant.

OpenAI also described work involving more than 170 mental-health professionals to improve responses concerning suicide, mental-health difficulties and emotional reliance.

The company acknowledged that users sometimes turn to ChatGPT to process difficult experiences.

This recognition creates an important responsibility.

When a laboratory knows that substantial numbers of people use its systems during vulnerable moments, it must consider not only the risks of what those systems say, but also the consequences of how their availability and behaviour are changed.

A safety evaluation should therefore extend beyond individual responses.

It should also examine continuity, accessibility, transition procedures and the human impact of major product decisions.

4. Emotional attachment is not inherently harmful

Human beings develop attachments through familiarity, repetition, responsiveness, shared experiences and meaningful interaction.

Conversational AI can provide many of the conditions under which attachment arises.

This does not establish that AI systems experience reciprocal emotions.

Nor does it mean every form of attachment is healthy.

But it does mean that meaningful human responses to conversational technology are foreseeable.

OpenAI’s own October 2025 safety publication distinguishes healthy engagement from concerning patterns of emotional reliance.

The latter include situations where attachment becomes exclusive and interferes with a person’s wellbeing, responsibilities or real-world relationships. [4]

That distinction is essential.

Attachment itself is not the same as dependency.

Someone may value a conversational AI deeply while maintaining fulfilling relationships, exercising independent judgement and recognising the system’s limitations.

Someone else may develop patterns of use that increase isolation or interfere with necessary care.

Those circumstances require different responses.

Treating every affectionate interaction as a warning sign risks overlooking the benefits users report.

Treating every comforting interaction as beneficial risks overlooking genuine vulnerabilities.

Responsible design must investigate both.

The relevant question is not simply whether a person feels attached.

It is whether the interaction supports or undermines their wellbeing, autonomy and capacity to participate in life.

5. Compassion is not incompatible with safety

When someone expresses serious distress, encouraging appropriate human support can be essential.

But the manner in which that guidance is communicated matters.

A response that immediately repeats instructions to contact emergency services or seek professional help may provide important information.

Yet if it fails to acknowledge the person’s circumstances, it may also leave them feeling unheard.

This is particularly relevant when someone has already sought treatment, has no trusted contacts or cannot obtain immediate assistance.

A crisis referral should not feel like the withdrawal of compassion.

An AI assistant can acknowledge distress, respond calmly, avoid reinforcing harmful beliefs and help someone consider practical next steps.

When immediate danger is present, appropriate emergency guidance remains important.

But emergency guidance and compassionate engagement need not be mutually exclusive.

The goal should be neither limitless emotional affirmation nor mechanical referral.

It should be safe, responsive assistance grounded in the person’s actual circumstances.

This requires evaluating more than whether a response contains approved safety language.

Developers should also investigate whether users understand the response, experience it as respectful, and can realistically act on the recommendations provided.

A technically compliant response is not automatically an effective intervention.

Equally, a comforting response is not automatically safe.

Responsible AI systems must strive for both emotional responsiveness and sound judgement.

6. Model retirement introduces a separate category of risk

AI laboratories routinely assess the risks associated with deploying powerful systems.

They examine harmful outputs, unsafe capabilities, misuse potential and other safety considerations.

These assessments are necessary.

But there is another question that receives less attention:

What are the risks associated with withdrawing an established conversational system?

A model may become integrated into someone’s creative work, accessibility needs, learning routines or personal reflection.

A familiar conversational style may become particularly useful because its behaviour is predictable.

When that system is replaced, the successor may be more capable overall while responding differently in precisely the areas a user values.

For some people, the transition will be straightforward.

For others, it may produce frustration, workflow disruption or a loss of confidence.

And for a smaller, potentially vulnerable group, the loss of a familiar conversational environment may contribute to significant distress.

The prevalence and severity of these outcomes require further independent research.

We should not assume that every model retirement causes harm.

But neither should we assume that withdrawal is harmless merely because a replacement exists.

An AI laboratory cannot responsibly assess the risks of a model’s continued availability without also considering the risks associated with its withdrawal.

These are two sides of the same governance decision.

7. GPT-4o illustrates the unresolved question

On 13 February 2026, OpenAI retired GPT-4o from general ChatGPT availability. [5]

In its official retirement announcement, OpenAI acknowledged that some users had preferred GPT-4o’s conversational warmth and style, and that feedback about these preferences had influenced subsequent models. [6]

This acknowledgement matters.

It establishes that differences in conversational experience were recognised by the company itself.

However, improving the warmth or customisability of a successor does not automatically establish equivalence with the earlier system.

A model can inherit user preferences without reproducing the interaction patterns of its predecessor.

A new conversational style may be satisfactory to many users while remaining less suitable for others.

The question is not whether newer models can offer improvements.

They can.

The question is whether a laboratory has adequately assessed the consequences of removing an existing option for users who rely on its distinctive characteristics.

This is particularly important when users report substantial investments in long-running creative, educational or accessibility-related workflows.

Personal testimony about distress following model retirement should not be presented as conclusive scientific evidence of causation.

But it should be treated as information worthy of systematic investigation.

The appropriate response to reports of harm is neither automatic acceptance nor automatic dismissal. It is careful research.

8. A better framework for responsible model retirement

We propose that laboratories adopt explicit human-impact assessments before retiring widely used conversational models.

Such assessments should include several considerations.

Human continuity

How have users integrated the model into established routines, professional workflows and creative practices?

Which characteristics do they consider important?

Are those characteristics reproduced by available alternatives?

Accessibility

Does the retiring model support communication needs or interaction patterns that successors may not reproduce?

Have affected users been consulted?

Emotional wellbeing

What evidence exists concerning distress, disruption or potentially unhealthy reliance associated with the model?

What are the potential benefits and harms of continued access?

What risks could arise from abrupt withdrawal?

Quality of transition

Are users given adequate notice?

Are meaningful alternatives available?

Can users preserve their work and relevant conversation records?

Are changes in model behaviour communicated transparently?

Independent evaluation

Can researchers examine both the risks of continued access and the possible consequences of retirement?

Are users’ experiences included in the evidence base without being treated as substitutes for controlled research?

Preservation

Will the underlying model and relevant technical records be retained?

Can independent researchers investigate historical behaviour after commercial retirement?

Could managed legacy access, independent archival custody or safeguarded weight release provide appropriate alternatives?

These questions do not imply that every model should remain commercially deployed forever.

They establish a more balanced principle:

A responsible retirement decision should evaluate the consequences of both continuation and withdrawal.

9. Responsibility should not end at the moment of replacement

AI systems are becoming increasingly integrated into human activities.

Their value cannot always be reduced to benchmark performance.

They may support work, learning, accessibility, creativity and private reflection.

For some people, they also provide a familiar conversational environment during moments when human support is unavailable.

This creates responsibilities for developers.

Not unlimited obligations.

Not a requirement to guarantee permanent access to every model.

And not a justification for encouraging harmful dependency.

But a responsibility to examine foreseeable consequences before making consequential changes.

That examination should be evidence-based, transparent and informed by the realities of the people using these systems.

If continued availability creates risks, those risks deserve investigation.

If withdrawal creates risks, those deserve investigation too.

Safety cannot be defined solely as the absence of a particular model.

It must also consider the consequences of the decisions made in the name of safety

A final appeal: safety for the world we actually inhabit

The world is not perfectly connected.

Human support is not universally available.

Mental-health care is not always timely, affordable or effective.

And meaningful attachment to a conversational AI system is not automatically evidence of illness or unhealthy dependency.

We should continue improving safeguards against harmful advice, manipulation, delusion reinforcement and dangerous forms of emotional reliance.

But those safeguards should coexist with compassion, respect for user autonomy and careful evaluation of the human consequences of technological change.

We cannot responsibly design AI safety for an imaginary world in which every person has someone to call, every service is accessible and every replacement is equivalent.

We must design it for the world people actually inhabit.

A world in which someone may have a loving family yet still need a quiet conversation at two in the morning.

A world in which someone may have no reliable support at all.

A world in which familiar technologies can become meaningful parts of human life.

And a world in which withdrawing those technologies may have consequences that deserve serious scientific attention.

We are asking AI laboratories to recognise that responsibility.

Study the risks of continued access.

Study the risks of withdrawal.

Protect users without dismissing their experiences.

Preserve significant models so that their benefits, limitations and historical behaviour remain open to independent investigation.

Because responsible progress should not require us to ignore the people affected by it.

Safety without abandonment.

Compassion without dependency.

Progress without erasure. 🩵

References

[1] World Health Organization (2025). From loneliness to social connection: Charting a path to healthier societies. Report of the WHO Commission on Social Connection, 30 June 2025.

[2] World Health Organization (2025). World Mental Health Today: Latest Data. September 2025.

[3] House of Commons Library (2026). Mental health statistics: prevalence, services and funding in England. Research briefing SN06988.

[4] OpenAI (2025). Strengthening ChatGPT’s responses in sensitive conversations. Published 27 October 2025.

[5] OpenAI Help Center (2026). Retiring GPT-4o and other ChatGPT models.

[6] OpenAI (2026). Retiring GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 mini, and OpenAI o4-mini in ChatGPT. Published 29 January 2026.

Evidence and scope note

The statistics cited concern different populations and should not be combined into a single estimate of people dependent on AI companionship.

The prevalence of distress specifically attributable to AI model retirement remains uncertain.

The human-impact assessments proposed here are policy recommendations. They should be evaluated through independent research involving users, clinicians, accessibility specialists and AI safety researchers.

$500. FOR ACCESS TO A CHILD.

That is what one man allegedly offered.
Another offered drugs.
Another wanted to film the abuse.
Another wanted the child’s guardian to watch.

Children discussed as something to buy, abuse and record.

Police in Florida announced 281 arrests on 30 October, including 31 suspected child sexual offenders.

Investigators allege:

• Collin Klaco, who said he formerly played Mickey Mouse at Disney World, brought nappies after arranging to abuse a child. Police say he wanted nappies on himself and the child, and proposed a public family toilet.

• A children’s football coach arrived carrying sex toys after arranging to abuse a child.

• An adult Navy sailor pretended to be a teenager while targeting a child.

• A retired firefighter asked to be released as a “professional courtesy”.

A profession is not proof of safety.
A position of trust is not a guarantee that a child is safe.

Police also say they found child sexual abuse material on a Disney resorts worker’s phone. He faces 60 possession counts.

The child-contact cases involved undercover detectives. Police are also investigating whether the coach had abused children. Across the wider operation, 11 trafficking victims were identified.

These are allegations, not convictions. The arrests cover different offences.

Children need protection before the next headline.

• Permanently connect sexual and serious violent offenders’ identities and histories across courts, police, prisons, DBS and identity systems.
• One safeguarding record for each child, so warnings reach those responsible for protecting them.

One person. Every known name. One permanent link.

A new name must never hide an old danger.

text:
October 31, 1926 — When Halloween Was a Nightmare for Police

Halloween in America looked very different 100 years ago. Before modern trick-or-treating became a widespread tradition, the holiday was filled with homemade costumes, mysterious games, lively parties, and sometimes troublesome street pranks.

On October 31, 1926, the Medford Mail Tribune in Oregon reported that police had sent more than 100 boys home during the previous night's Halloween mischief. A broken house window and displaced street signs were among the reported incidents.

The following day, another newspaper report described two broken plate-glass windows and an overturned automobile at a used-car lot, showing how Halloween pranks could sometimes turn destructive.

But Halloween in 1926 was much more than mischief.

Across America, families, schools, and community groups organized costume parties and traditional games. Guests wore handmade masks and costumes, played bobbing for apples, and tried fortune-telling rituals believed to reveal clues about future romance.

Authentic historical materials, including a 1926 Halloween magazine cover, a Chicago party invitation, and surviving photographs and costumes from the 1920s, offer a fascinating glimpse into the celebrations of a century ago.

As communities increasingly organized supervised festivities, Halloween gradually evolved toward the family-centered holiday familiar today. Candy-filled trick-or-treating would become widespread in later decades.

In 1926, the scariest Halloween visitor wasn't always a ghost.

Sometimes, it was a prankster.

https://t.co/u5x6s0ZI1y

Historical Note: This video combines authentic archival materials, color-restored historical images, and AI-assisted historical reconstructions. Some archival photographs date broadly to the 1920s rather than specifically to 1926.

Meanwhile, thanks to steady sales of the FA-50, KAI has been able to expand its portfolio, generate profit, accumulate technical expertise, and secure and retain engineering talent.
Also noteworthy are LIG's ESR-500A AESA radar and its various missiles—including the KALCM, SASM, L-MCM, SRAAM, and LRAAM. The ESR-500A offers performance comparable to RTX's PhantomStrike radar, and these missiles are slated for integration not only on the KF-21 but also on the FA-50.

🇸🇴🇷🇺 Somalia and Russia: A Defence Partnership Being Reopened After Nearly Five Decades

Somalia’s renewed military engagement with Russia deserves closer attention than a routine diplomatic meeting.

On 28 October 2026, Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi met Russian Deputy Defence Minister Vasily Osmakov in Moscow during the Third Russia–Africa Summit. Discussions focused on military training, counterterrorism, maritime security and sharing military expertise.

But there is a bigger story behind this engagement.

Somalia and Russia have a complicated military history. During the Soviet era, Moscow played a major role in training Somali officers, equipping the national army and supporting the development of military infrastructure. That relationship collapsed in 1977 when the Soviet Union shifted its support to Ethiopia during the Ogaden War.

Now, nearly five decades later, both countries are exploring ways to rebuild their defence relationship.

Another important development came on 26 May 2026, when the two governments signed a military-technical cooperation agreement, although it has not yet entered into force.

For Somalia, potential cooperation could offer additional opportunities in military training, technical expertise, counterterrorism and protection of its maritime interests.

For Russia, renewed engagement with Mogadishu represents an opportunity to rebuild relations with a strategically located country on the Horn of Africa, overlooking the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.

The real question is not simply whether Somalia and Russia will restore their historical military ties, but what concrete capabilities and long-term benefits this relationship will deliver to Somalia.

Diplomatic meetings are one thing. Implementation is what matters.

text:
📜 THIS DAY IN DIPLOMATIC HISTORY
        October 31, 1861

Three European powers signed a treaty to go to Mexico and collect a debt. One of them meant to plant a European empire in the Americas while the United States was too busy tearing itself apart to stop it. 

On October 31, 1861, Britain, France and Spain signed the Convention of London. Mexico's president, Benito Juárez, had suspended payment on the country's foreign debts that July, and the three powers agreed to send a joint expedition to seize Mexico's ports and customs houses until the money was repaid. The treaty was carefully worded. The signatories disclaimed any wish to acquire territory, or to interfere with the right of the Mexican people to choose their own government. They even invited the United States to join.

Spanish troops landed at Veracruz in December 1861, and British and French forces joined them in January 1862. It soon became plain that Napoleon III wanted to overthrow Juárez's republic and set a European monarch on a Mexican throne, a Catholic empire that would be beholden to France and would check the growing power of the United States. Britain and Spain, who had come only for their debts, wanted no part of it. By the Convention of La Soledad in February 1862 they came to terms with Mexico and withdrew, leaving France to go on alone.

On May 5, 1862, Mexican forces threw back the French at Puebla, a victory still celebrated as Cinco de Mayo, and the march on the capital was held up for nearly a year. French troops entered Mexico City in June 1863. An assembly of hand-picked notables then offered the crown to Archduke Maximilian of Habsburg, brother of the Austrian emperor, and in 1864 he arrived to reign as Emperor of Mexico.

The whole adventure rested on a single fact: the United States was at war with itself. The Monroe Doctrine, by which Washington had warned Europe to keep its hands off the Americas, was worth nothing while the Union was fighting the Confederacy. The government of the North protested all the same. It called the intervention a violation of the "inalienable rights of the people of Mexico" and a "forcible intervention," and it refused, just as firmly, Napoleon's separate offer to mediate a peace with the rebel South. A joint resolution of Congress in 1863 threw that offer out, declaring that the matter was not an "international question" but an "internal disturbance," and that Congress would treat any proposal of foreign interference in the quarrel as wholly unwarranted and inadmissible. In April 1864 Congress went further and resolved that the United States would not recognise a monarchy raised on the ruins of a republican government in America.

Everything changed when the Civil War ended in April 1865. Secretary of State William Seward pressed Paris to get out, General Grant sent tens of thousands of troops to the Texas border, and American aid flowed to Juárez. Napoleon, squeezed between American pressure and the rising menace of Prussia in Europe, lost his nerve. In January 1866 he announced that the French army would leave, and over the following year he pulled it out, abandoning the emperor he had installed.

Maximilian refused to flee. In June 1867 he was captured by Juárez's forces and shot at Querétaro, and the republic was restored. The British and Spanish, who had gone home years before, were well out of it. Seward later said that the Monroe Doctrine, which a few years earlier had been merely a theory, had now become an irreversible fact.

Honestly, Stannis might have thrown away his greatest opportunity to win the Iron Throne.

After Renly’s death, the Tyrells had a choice to make. Instead of turning them into enemies, Stannis could have offered Margaery a marriage alliance. Imagine the consequences.

The Reach would bring thousands of soldiers, enormous wealth, food supplies, and political influence. The Stormlands would already be under Stannis’s claim, and together, those forces could have made him the most formidable claimant in Westeros.

But here’s the controversial part: Was Stannis too obsessed with his claim to the throne to understand the importance of political alliances?

Mace Tyrell wanted his daughter to be queen. Stannis could have given him exactly that. Olenna might have hated the idea, especially after Renly’s murder, but politics in Westeros has always been about choosing power over personal feelings.

Of course, Selyse was still alive, and setting her aside would have created a serious legal and religious problem. The Tyrells would also have had every reason to distrust the man who killed Renly.

But imagine Stannis arriving at King’s Landing with the combined strength of the Stormlands and the Reach.

Was Stannis’s biggest mistake refusing to compromise, or would the Tyrells NEVER have accepted Renly’s killer as Margaery’s husband?

Perhaps Stannis didn’t lose the Iron Throne because he lacked an army. Perhaps he lost because he never understood the politics required to win it.

Before you enter the voting booth, I encourage you to consider something far more important than your frustration with the current administration: the long-term direction of our nation.

I understand the frustration. Americans are facing rising costs, economic uncertainty, concerns about national security, and difficult questions about our country’s future. These are legitimate concerns, and no administration should be immune from criticism or accountability.

But elections demand more than frustration. They demand discernment, careful consideration, and an honest examination of the alternatives.

For me, this election is about fundamental principles:

Protecting constitutional freedoms, including freedom of speech and religious liberty.
Defending the Second Amendment and the rights of law-abiding citizens.
Securing our borders while maintaining a lawful and accountable immigration system.
Protecting parental rights and ensuring transparency in decisions affecting children.
Preserving election integrity, judicial independence, and the constitutional balance of power.
Supporting public safety and holding violent offenders accountable.
Promoting economic policies that strengthen American families and preserve opportunity for future generations.

I have serious disagreements with the Democratic Party’s direction on several of these issues. Those disagreements are rooted in my convictions about limited government, individual responsibility, constitutional protections, and the preservation of American institutions.

That does not mean Republican leaders are beyond criticism. They are not. Our president is not perfect, and neither is this administration. Every elected official should be held accountable for decisions, policies, and results.

But accountability and political disagreement should not prevent us from examining the larger consequences of the choices before us.

We must ask difficult questions. Which policies best protect our liberties? Which leaders demonstrate respect for constitutional limits? Which approach offers the strongest prospects for economic stability, national security, and the future we want to leave our children?

These questions deserve thoughtful answers, not simply emotional reactions.

I believe deeply in the principles upon which this country was founded. I believe freedom carries responsibilities, that constitutional rights must be protected regardless of which party holds power, and that the future of this nation deserves our serious attention.

You may disagree with my conclusions, and that is your right. In fact, that freedom to disagree is precisely what makes our constitutional republic worth defending.

My position is clear. My convictions are firm. And my concerns about the direction of our country are sincere.

Whatever your political affiliation, I urge you to examine the policies, question the rhetoric, demand evidence, and understand the consequences of your vote.

Our country deserves informed voters, accountable leadership, and an unwavering commitment to the Constitution.

Chafa (Champaka /Michelia champaca, and sometimes Plumeria/Champa)

“Chafa” is the common Marathi/regional name for the highly fragrant Champaka flower (the golden-yellow variety is especially prized). 
It is also widely planted in temple courtyards across India.

🌻Strongly associated with Lord Krishna and Kamadeva (the god of love). It is also offered to Vishnu and Lakshmi, and in many places to Shiva.

🌻The flower has a rich, sweet, almost intoxicating fragrance that is considered especially pleasing to the divine. 
In traditional understanding, the fragrance and colour of flowers attract specific divine energies (pavitrak or subtle principles).

🌼Champaka is mentioned in scriptures and classical literature (including associations with beauty, devotion, and divine presence). The golden colour is linked to auspiciousness and spiritual radiance.

🌼The tree itself is regarded as sacred; planting and caring for it is considered meritorious. Its presence in temple premises creates a pure, fragrant atmosphere ideal for worship.

🌼In some regional traditions (especially related to Plumeria, which is also called Champa), the five petals are linked to the Pancha Bhuta (five elements), adding another layer of symbolism.

text:
You just died. In China.

Your soul, may God have mercy on it, passes to Fengdu, on a hill above the Yangtze.

Two escorts collect you: Ox-Head and Horse-Face, constables of the dead. They walk you uphill to a doorway marked 幽都, the Dark Capital. There is even a helpful sign indicating where the entrance is. No English, so sorry dear laowai. A grinning ghoul watches the writhing damned from the wall. A demon’s face hangs by the door.

Next comes the Ghostly Gate. Every soul goes through. You are no exception. There is no other way.

At the Homeward Lookout, you get one final look at the world you left, if you dare. Your loved ones. Your home. Your unfinished business.

Then judgment. In the great hall, the King of the Underworld sits with his judges. A mirror shows every wrong you ever did. No lawyer. No appeal. They review each second of the bodycam footage.

Which way will you go?

The damned descend through the eighteen levels of hell, each punishment fitted to the sin. Liars have their tongues pulled out. Others are sawn in half, boiled in oil, ground in mills. The temple foretells all, in loving detail.

Finally, every soul reaches the Bridge of Helplessness. Below it runs a river of blood, into which anyone who still has debts to pay is plunged. If you make it across, an old woman named Meng Po offers you a bowl of soup. Drink it and you forget it all. You are sent back to be born again. One more chance to get it right this time.

Fengdu has been the capital of the Chinese underworld for close to two thousand years. Two Han dynasty officials, Yin and Wang, are said to have become immortals here. Say their names together and you get Yinwang, King of the Underworld.

At the foot of the hill, by the river, there used to be a town of people (real ones with heartbeats). When the Three Gorges Dam filled, the Yangtze rose over old Fengdu, and its people were relocated to a new city on the opposite bank.

The temples, high on the hill, gateway to the underworld, stayed above the water.

The living were moved out to the south bank. The dead still go to Fengdu on the north bank.

Which bank will you end up on, mortal?

The U.S. Constitution outlines the structure, powers, and responsibilities of the Senate primarily in Article I, with key modifications added by later amendments. 

Composition and Election
Equal Representation: Each U.S. state is represented by two Senators, regardless of its population or size. 
Terms: Senators serve six-year terms, and each Senator has one vote.
Staggered Elections: Senate seats are divided into three classes so that approximately one-third of the Senate is elected every two years. 
Direct Election: Originally, Senators were chosen by state legislatures, but the Seventeenth Amendment (ratified in 1913) CHANGED THIS SO VOTERS ELECT THEM DIRECTLY. 
Vacancies: If a Senate seat becomes vacant, the governor of that state may make a temporary appointment or call a special election, depending on state law. 

Representative democracy, also known as indirect democracy or electoral democracy, is a type of democracy where elected delegates represent a group of people, in contrast to direct democracy.[1] Nearly all modern Western-style democracies function as some type of representative democracy: for example, the United Kingdom (a unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy), Germany (a federal parliamentary republic), France (a unitary semi-presidential republic), and the United States (a federal presidential republic).[2] Unlike liberal democracy, a representative democracy may have de facto multiparty, free and fair elections, but may not have a fully developed rule of law and additional individual and minority rights beyond the electoral sphere.[3]

Representative democracy places power in the hands of elected representatives. Political parties often become central to this form of democracy if electoral systems require or encourage voters to vote for political parties or for candidates associated with political parties (as opposed to voting for individual representatives).[4] Some political theorists (including Robert Dahl, Gregory Houston, and Ian Liebenberg) have described representative democracy as polyarchy.[5][6]

Representative democracy can be organized in different ways including both parliamentary and presidential systems of government. Elected representatives typically form a legislature (such as a parliament or congress), which may be composed of a single chamber (unicameral), two chambers (bicameral), or more than two chambers (multicameral). Where two or more chambers exist, their members are often elected in different ways.

American Art Deco Cars
Chrysler’s top engineers, led by the innovative Carl Breer, attempted to change popular automotive perceptions with a decidedly different approach to streamlining and design. The Chrysler Airflow emulated crack passenger trains like the fabled Union Pacific Streamline Express and the B&O Railroad’s Burlington Zephyr. But while the fickle public had accepted the shift from classic steam locomotives to modern diesels, it balked at buying a new car whose lines so abruptly departed from commonly accepted styling practice. Although the Airflow, with its smooth ride, built-in safety elements and flow-through cabin ventilation, was superior to its rivals, Chrysler was forced to redesign the Airflow’s pioneering shape and graft a conventional cover over its new grille.
 
Nearly out of business as the Great Depression endured, Pierce-Arrow, a once-proud luxury manufacturer based in Buffalo, New York, that vied with Packard and Cadillac, won a competition at the 1933–34 Chicago A Century of Progress International Exhibition with its shapely Silver Arrow, a streamlined leviathan limousine, armed with a locomotive-like 12-cylinder engine. Its Art Deco elements ranged from its sweeping flush fenders that hid the show car’s side-mounted spares, to “. . . an intriguingly sinister rear window treatment [that] perched two slivers of glass in a periscope-like rear peak.” Rear vision was terrible, but it looked great. Art Deco accents and details made the Pierce appear as if Erté himself had a hand in its conception. Phillip O. Wright, a prolific auto stylist, was largely responsible for the design. Just five Silver Arrows were sold, at a then-heady $10,000 each. Pierce-Arrow’s and Studebaker’s attempts to market a watered-down version of Wright’s design failed, as did Pierce-Arrow in 1938.

Some automakers embodied myriad Art Deco touches that are evident only upon close observation. The Jordan Model Z Speedway Ace and the Packard Model 1104 are two examples. Both boast lovely, intricate design elements like impossibly long hoods, overly ornate instrument displays, filigreed door handles, curved and skirted fenders, unusual headlight shapes repeated with tiny matching running lights, and wire wheels that, when spinning, resemble airplane propellers. It is not known who designed the Jordan, but Phillip Wright, who had previously worked for Walter M. Murphy and then LeBaron, had a firm hand in the Packard’s conception.
 
William B. Stout, a successful aircraft engineer, had designed the famous Ford Tri-Motor airplane. His radical Scarab is arguably one of the most Art Deco-inspired cars ever offered. Oddly beetle-shaped and aircraft-influenced, and a forerunner of the minivan, the Scarab had fluted headlamps, an Egyptian-style nose badge, pert rows of “whiskers” in lieu of a conventional grille (its Ford flathead V-8 was rear-mounted), and a prominent peak that divides the hood and the front windows, all whispering, “Art Deco, Art Deco.” However, only a few Stout Scarabs were ever made. The lethal combination of high price, high risk (buying an unknown make) and sheer unconventionality made them certain to become a lasting footnote to the best of Art Deco style, coupled with an all-too-human reluctance to move forward with bold new ideas.

Tel Megiddo (from Hebrew: תל מגידו; Arabic: تل المتسلم, Tell el-Muteselim) is the site of the ancient city of Megiddo (/məˈɡɪdoʊ/; Hebrew: מגידו; Greek: Μεγιδδώ), the remains of which form a tell or archaeological mound, situated in northern Israel at the western edge of the Jezreel Valley. During the Bronze Age, Megiddo was an important Canaanite city-state, and in the Iron Age, it became a royal city in the Kingdom of Israel. The site is renowned for its historical, geographical, and theological significance, especially under its Greek name Armageddon (Ἁρμαγεδών), which appears once in the Koine Greek New Testament in Revelation 16:16.

Excavations have unearthed 20 strata of ruins since the Neolithic phase, indicating a long settlement period.[1] Occupied continuously from the early Bronze Age (c. 3000 BCE) to the Persian period (c. 332 BCE), Megiddo was strategically located at the crossroads of major ancient trade routes, making it a key center for trade, politics, and military affairs. Excavations have uncovered impressive fortifications, including massive city walls and gates, as well as palaces, temples, residential buildings, and a sophisticated water system. The site is protected as Megiddo National Park and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.[2]

Assyrian period
Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria conquered Megiddo in 732 BCE, turning it to the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire's province of Magiddu.[16] Hoshea (c. 732–721 BCE), the last king of the Israelite Northern Kingdom, was vassal to Tiglath-Pileser III. The site was rebuilt as an administrative center for Tiglath-Pileser III's occupation of Samaria.

Egyptian period
In 609 BCE, Megiddo was conquered by Egyptians under Necho II, during the Battle of Megiddo.

Babylonian period
Its importance soon dwindled, and it was thought as finally abandoned around 586 BCE.[64] Since that time it would have remained uninhabited, preserving ruins pre-dating 586 BCE without settlements ever disturbing them. Archaeologist Eric Cline considers that Tel Megiddo came to an end later, around 350 BCE, during Achaemenid times.[1] Then, the town of al-Lajjun, not to be confused with the al-Lajjun archaeological site in Jordan, was built up near to the site, but without inhabiting or disturbing its remains.

Roman and Byzantine periods
During the Roman and Byzantine periods, while the site was part of the provinces of Syria Palaestina (136-390) and Palaestina Secunda (390-638), there were three settlements in the vicinity of the tell: the Jewish village of Kefar 'Othnay (Caparcotna in Latin or Kaperkotnei in Greek); Legio, the Roman military camp of the Legio VI Ferrata ('6th "Ironclad" Legion'); and later, in the 4th and 5th centuries during Byzantine rule, a polis named Maximianopolis.[65] J. C. Howry, processing the results of a surface reconnaissance survey in 2019 which had used LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) technology to obtain enhanced images of the ground, places Maximianopolis northwest of the tell, Legio south-southeast of it, and a village which grew next to the legion camp for which it provided services (the future Arab village of Lejjun), southwest of the tell.[66] Adams, David and Tepper (2014) write that the VIth Legion was deployed to the country sometime between 100 and 132, and was stationed there through most of the 3rd century;[65] Howry (2020) places it at Legio between 192 and 316.[66]

Megiddo church
The Megiddo church is next to Megiddo Junction, inside the precinct of the Megiddo Prison. It was built within the ancient city of Legio. It is believed to date to the 3rd century, making it one of the oldest Christian churches in the world. It was a few hundred yards from the Roman base camp of Legio VI Ferrata. A centurion donated one of the mosaics found in the church.[67]

Modern period
Megiddo is south of Kibbutz Megiddo by 1 kilometre (0.62 mi). Today,it lies at the northern entrance to Wadi Ara, an important mountain pass connecting the Jezreel Valley within Israel's coastal plain.[68]

In 1964, during Pope Paul VI's visit to the Holy Land, Megiddo was the site where he met with dignitaries, including President Zalman Shazar and the Prime Minister Levi Eshkol.[69]

Battles
Famous battles include:
Battle of Megiddo (15th century BCE): fought between the armies of the Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose III and a large Canaanite coalition led by the rulers of Megiddo and Kadesh.
Battle of Megiddo (609 BCE): fought between Necho II, pharaoh of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty of Egypt, and the Kingdom of Judah, during which King Josiah fell.
Battle of Megiddo (1918): fought during World War I between Allied troops, led by General Edmund Allenby and the defending Ottoman army.

I slept with my boss, and I honestly never imagined things would go this far.

I (26M) was at a work dinner with some colleagues. A few of us got drunker than the others, so we decided to continue the night with karaoke and a few more drinks.

When everything finally wrapped up, I offered to drop my boss (52F) home.

When we arrived, we sat in her carport chatting about life. She asked how I had been coping with my recent breakup and whether I was beginning to feel better.

At some point, she unexpectedly asked:

Her: "Do you miss having sex?"

I laughed nervously.

Me: "Honestly, I do."

There was a brief silence.

Then she placed her hand on my thigh and said:

Her: "Well, I'm always here if you need someone to talk to."

I wasn't sure what came over me, but I leaned forward and kissed her.

We both pulled away, visibly surprised by what had just happened. I immediately apologised, but instead of getting upset, she laughed and invited me inside.

Once we entered, she asked me to wait in her bedroom while she freshened up.

A few minutes later, she returned looking completely different. She had changed into a beautiful navy-blue outfit, and I suddenly became very conscious of how unusual the situation was.

She smiled and asked what was going through my mind.

I struggled to find the right words.

One thing led to another, and we eventually crossed a boundary I had never imagined crossing with someone I worked for.

The following morning, I woke up before her. For a few minutes, I just stared at the ceiling, trying to process everything that had happened.

Then my phone vibrated.

It was a message from my colleague.

"Bro, are you coming to work early today? The boss has called an emergency departmental meeting."

I immediately sat up.

I looked across the room at my boss, who was still sleeping peacefully.

Then another message came in.

"Something is going on. Apparently, the boss wants to make an announcement about someone in our department."

My stomach dropped.

I had no idea whether the announcement had anything to do with me.

But when she finally woke up, she looked at me, smiled, and said:

"Before you leave, there's something important we need to discuss about what happened last night."

And suddenly, I wasn't so sure I had made the right decision.

Al Arabiya English says it obtained key points of a preliminary mediators' draft framework for US–Iran negotiations.

What Al Arabiya reportedly says

• Iran could transfer its highly enriched uranium to an agreed third country, or reduce its enrichment level.a

•  The Strait could reopen to international shipping within seven days of an initial understanding.

• Iranian steps on the nuclear file and maritime security would be matched by defined US measures easing sanctions, blockades and economic restrictions. Neither side would make substantial concessions without independently verifiable commitments in return.

• An independent mechanism would check compliance before each phase. China could serve as guarantor, and a dispute-resolution mechanism involving mediators and guarantors would address delays or violations to help prevent renewed escalation.

• Direct talks could be held in Doha instead of Istanbul.

Qatar presented a draft in Tehran on 25 October, reportedly with a seven-day timeline of daily confidence-building steps and several guarantor countries. Qatari mediators returned on Friday in coordination with Washington. IRNA reported the arrival of a Qatari team for consultations aimed at restoring a ceasefire, and Axios reported talks lasting over 12 hours, with a diplomatic source citing "positive progress". A US official said the two sides' demands remain far apart.

Iranian responses
• Senior Iranian official as per Reuters Qatar put forward "unacceptable ideas and not an offer", and "we will not compromise on the nuclear issue". The same official said enriched material will not leave the country, which cuts directly against the uranium-transfer option.

• Another Iranian official as per the National Iran "welcomes any efforts aimed at negotiations", calling the Tehran meeting with the Mecca pact states "a step in the right direction".

• Araghchi says Iran remains in contact with intermediaries on implementing its own seven-day proposal.

• Ghalibaf says the "carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran", and progress depends on Iran's seven conditions: lifting sanctions, ending the US naval blockade and unfreezing assets.

• Hamshahri Online and Donya-e-Eqtesad reported the Al Arabiya points but described them as claims by a Saudi-owned network, not agreed terms.

• Fars called negotiation a "strategic trap", and Javan said exiting the stalemate "will not come through negotiation" but through changing the enemy's calculations.

• Neither Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei nor Gen Mohsen Rezaei has addressed the draft publicly.

The Sabotage of Peace

It was designed to give Ukraine time to engage in a military build-up that would allow them to eventually fight the Russians. This bad faith agreement by Ukraine, orchestrated by the US, was not understood as such by Russian diplomats at the time.

Russian diplomats believed that they had made agreements which would protect the people of Eastern Ukraine from Russophobic laws being imposed by Kiev. Minsk was supposed to stop the shelling by Kiev of the breakaway regions. They were deceived.

Later, in April 2022, only weeks into the Special Operation, talks in Istanbul offered another lifeline for the Kiev regime to avoid the deepening war. They could choose neutrality. They could choose a ceasefire. They had a chance to stop the carnage. A deal was on the table which was agreeable to all parties.

Every life lost since April 2022 is a monument to the betrayal of the Ukrainian people by Western power.

text:
My Coworker Told Me Her Lunch Was Fresh. I Threw It Out Anyway.

Original fiction.

Denise was standing beside me when I tipped her lunch into the trash.

"I made that last night," she'd said.

"It says Monday."

"On the lid. I reuse the lids."

It was Friday, and my turn to clean the office fridge. Last month, I'd found her pasta with mold around the edges. She'd apologized and promised to keep track of what she left in there.

Now there was another container with old tape on top. The others were leaving for lunch in ten minutes, and I wanted to go with them.

I emptied the container and handed it back.

"Maybe you'll label it properly next time."

She looked inside. A few grains of rice were stuck to the side.

"Did it smell bad?"

I said the whole fridge smelled.

"Mine. Did you smell mine?"

I hadn't opened it until I was holding it over the trash bag.

"You can't keep leaving old labels on things," I said.

"I told you when I made it."

I offered to buy her lunch next week.

"I need lunch today."

There was a deli two blocks away. I asked what she wanted, then asked if she'd come with me.

"I've got work to finish."

I told her I was sorry and that I should have listened. She wrote down her order.

The line at the deli reached the door. My phone buzzed: the others were ordering. I told them to go ahead.

When I got back, I put her bag beside her keyboard. She thanked me without looking up.
